title: Welcome to OMFS
quote: The first job of the OMFS DCT is not to know everything—it is to recognise the sick patient, provide safe initial management, and know when to ask for help.

items:
Why This Matters
Starting an OMFS post can feel daunting. Unlike dental practice, OMFS combines dentistry, medicine and surgery. Within a single shift you may assess facial trauma, drain an odontogenic infection, review a tracheostomy, assist in theatre, manage ward patients, and receive referrals from emergency departments, general dental practitioners, GPs and other hospital specialties. No one expects a new DCT to know everything on day one. They do expect you to be organised, systematic, safe, and willing to escalate concerns early.

sections.heading: Golden Rule
items: Airway always comes first. A patient with a dental infection can deteriorate rapidly if the airway becomes compromised.

sections.heading: Core Content
items:
What is OMFS?
Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery (OMFS) is the surgical specialty concerned with the diagnosis and management of diseases, injuries and abnormalities affecting the mouth, teeth, jaws, face, neck, salivary glands, facial skin, and oral mucosa.

Most UK OMFS units also contribute to the management of: facial trauma, head and neck cancer, deep neck space infections, complex dentoalveolar surgery, orthognathic surgery, cleft surgery, craniofacial surgery, facial deformity, TMJ surgery, skin cancer.

sections.heading: Your Role as a DCT
items:
What Your Consultant Expects
Consultants do not expect you to know every diagnosis. They do expect you to: be punctual, be polite, know your patients, prioritise safety, escalate concerns promptly, keep accurate documentation, be honest if you do not know something.

sections.heading: The Golden Rules of OMFS
items: Assess the patient—not the X-ray. Never let imaging replace a thorough history and examination.
Airway always comes first. A patient with a dental problem can wait. A patient with an airway problem cannot.
Pain rarely kills. Airway obstruction, sepsis and haemorrhage do. Learn to identify immediately life-threatening problems before focusing on pain relief.
Never be afraid to escalate. Registrars and consultants would rather receive ten unnecessary calls than miss one patient with impending airway compromise.
Good documentation protects patients. If it is not documented, it may be assumed not to have happened.

sections.heading: Is the patient stable? Assess airway, breathing, circulation
items: Why has OMFS been called? Clarify exact reason: swelling, trauma, bleeding, dental pain, oral lesion
Does this patient need immediate review? Airway compromise, active haemorrhage, visual disturbance, neurological deficit, sepsis
What information do I need before I attend? Referrer name, patient details, location, observations, imaging, blood results, referrer's concern

sections.heading: Rapidly spreading facial swelling
items:
DCT Checklist: First Week Essentials
□ How to contact the registrar
□ How to contact the consultant
□ How to access radiology
□ How to request blood tests
□ How to request imaging
□ Where emergency airway equipment is kept
□ Local antibiotic guidance
□ Theatre timetable
□ Ward routine
□ Referral pathway

sections.heading: Consultant Pearls 💡
items: The best DCTs are not necessarily the most knowledgeable—they are the most reliable
Always introduce yourself to nursing staff. They will often recognise deterioration before anyone else
Review imaging yourself before discussing it with a senior but never rely on the image alone

sections.heading: Key Takeaways
items: Patient safety always comes first — airway, sepsis and haemorrhage are your priority emergencies

sections.heading: Good documentation and communication are as important as clinical knowledge
items: Your role is safe initial assessment — begin appropriate management and seek senior support when needed

Registrar Handover Prompt
Before phoning the registrar, be ready to answer: Who is the patient? Why have they been referred? What are the observations? Is the airway safe? What does the examination show? What investigations have been performed? What is your working diagnosis? What management have you started? What do you want from the registrar?

title: Your First On-call Shift
quote: The purpose of your first on-call is not to manage every patient independently. Your job is to assess patients safely, recognise the unwell patient, initiate appropriate management and escalate appropriately.

items:
Why This Matters
For many DCTs, the first on-call shift is the most daunting part of starting OMFS. The bleep may seem relentless, referrals can arrive simultaneously from multiple departments, and many patients will have medical as well as dental problems. Remember that you are never expected to work in isolation. The registrar and consultant are there to support you, and early escalation is a sign of good judgement—not weakness.

sections.heading: Golden Rule
items: Never let the bleep dictate your priorities. The loudest referral is not necessarily the sickest patient. Always ask: Who needs me first?

sections.heading: Core Content
items:
Before Your Shift Starts
Arrive 15–20 minutes early. Ensure you know: registrar's name/contact, consultant on call, how to contact anaesthetic team, ED/theatres/wards/radiology locations, PACS/EPR access, local antibiotic guidelines, emergency theatre pathway, CEPOD booking. Carry: hospital bleep, charged phone, ID badge, pen, notebook.

sections.heading: Prioritising Referrals
items:
Receiving a Telephone Referral
Record: referrer name/designation, patient name, hospital number, age, location, responsible consultant. Ask: "What is your specific concern?" Clarify exactly why OMFS input is required. Get: current observations, NEWS2, airway status. Never assume the patient is stable.

Your First Assessment
Step 1: ABCDE assessment
Step 2: Focused history
Step 3: Targeted examination
Step 4: Review imaging — never rely solely on report
Step 5: Formulate working diagnosis, differentials, immediate plan
Step 6: Decide: admit, discharge, discuss, operate?

sections.heading: Any uncertainty — if you are worried, call
items:
DCT Checklist: Before Finishing Every Referral
□ Have I assessed the airway?
□ Have I recorded the observations?
□ Have I documented the history and examination?
□ Have I reviewed any available imaging?
□ Have I started appropriate initial management?
□ Have I discussed with my senior if indicated?
□ Have I documented the outcome of that discussion?
□ Does the patient need review again?

End of Shift Checklist
Before handing over: ensure all outstanding referrals reviewed/handed over, document pending investigations, highlight unstable patients, communicate anticipated problems, confirm responsibility for follow-up actions.

sections.heading: Consultant Pearls 💡
items: The patient who appears "too well" may still deteriorate quickly—repeat assessments are often more informative than a single examination

sections.heading: Read the CT yourself before discussing it with your registrar
items: If you have not examined the patient, avoid making management decisions over the telephone

sections.heading: Prepare before speaking to your registrar by gathering all relevant information
items: Clear documentation and effective handover are as important as clinical decision-making

Registrar Handover Prompt
Before calling: patient age, relevant medical history, mechanism/complaint, observations, airway status, examination findings, imaging findings, blood results, working diagnosis, proposed plan. A concise presentation allows timely decisions.

title: How to Clerk an OMFS Patient
quote: A good clerking tells the patient's story, demonstrates your clinical reasoning and allows any member of the team to safely continue their care.

items:
Why This Matters
Clerking is one of the most important skills you will develop during your OMFS rotation. A structured assessment not only supports accurate diagnosis and management but also provides a clear record of your clinical reasoning. Well-documented clerkings improve communication, facilitate safe handovers and protect both patients and clinicians. Your role is not simply to document findings but to identify the patient's immediate problems, recognise red flags and formulate an initial management plan.

sections.heading: Golden Rule
items: Use the same structured clerking format for every patient. Tailor your history and examination to the presenting complaint while never overlooking the airway or vital signs.

sections.heading: The OMFS Clerking Framework
items: Patient Details, 2. Presenting Complaint, 3. History of Presenting Complaint, 4. Medical History, 5. Drug History, 6. Allergies, 7. Social History, 8. Dental History, 9. Examination, 10. Investigations, 11. Differential Diagnosis, 12. Impression, 13. Management Plan. If you always follow the same format, you are far less likely to omit important information.

Examination Must-Haves
Always begin with: General Assessment — NEWS2, temperature, hydration, distress.
Extraoral: facial symmetry, swelling, bruising, lacerations, skin changes, tenderness, fluctuance, bony step, lymph nodes, cranial nerves, eye movements, visual acuity if trauma.
Intraoral: oral hygiene, dentition, soft tissues, floor of mouth, tongue, palate, uvula, occlusion, mouth opening in mm, source tooth.
Never forget: airway assessment, maximum inter-incisal opening in infection/trauma.

sections.heading: Red Flags ⚠️
items: Airway: stridor, drooling, trismus <15mm, floor of mouth elevation, voice change

sections.heading: Trauma: malocclusion, open fracture, step deformity, infraorbital paraesthesia
items:
DCT Clerking Checklist
Before leaving the patient, confirm documented: □ Presenting complaint, □ Full history, □ Medical history, □ Drug history, □ Allergies, □ Social history, □ Dental history, □ Observations, □ Complete examination, □ Relevant investigations, □ Differential diagnosis, □ Impression, □ Management plan, □ Senior discussion

sections.heading: Consultant Pearls 💡
items: Relevant negatives are as important as positive findings. Documenting no dysphagia, no voice change, no floor of mouth elevation is valuable

sections.heading: Never copy previous notes without confirming findings yourself
items: If you think a patient is deteriorating, document the change and reassess rather than relying on initial clerking

sections.heading: Key Takeaways
items: Use the same structured format for every patient — consistency prevents omissions

sections.heading: Summarise clinical reasoning with differential diagnosis and impression
items: A concise, well-organised clerking improves patient safety and demonstrates professionalism

Registrar Handover Prompt
Before calling, know: airway status, observations, key findings, imaging, bloods, working diagnosis, initial management, specific question. Aim to summarise in under one minute.

title: Receiving and Managing OMFS Referrals
quote: A good referral is the beginning of good patient care. Your job is to establish why the patient has been referred, determine how urgently they need to be seen, and ensure they receive the right care at the right time.

items:
Why This Matters
Every on-call shift revolves around referrals. Some require immediate intervention, while others can safely wait. The ability to receive a structured referral, identify red flags, prioritise competing demands and communicate effectively with both referrers and senior colleagues is one of the defining skills of a competent OMFS DCT. Never accept a referral without understanding exactly what is being asked of you.

sections.heading: Golden Rule
items: Never start by asking, "Which tooth?" Start by asking: "Is the patient stable?" The airway and physiological status always come before the dental diagnosis.

sections.heading: The OMFS Referral Framework: REFERRAL
items:
Prioritising Referrals
Immediate: Airway compromise, active haemorrhage, orbital compartment syndrome, deep neck infection, septic patient, expanding neck swelling — discuss with registrar without delay.
Urgent: Mandibular fracture, facial laceration, dental trauma, facial cellulitis, suspected orbital fracture — usually within one hour.
Routine: Dental pain, dry socket, chronic TMJ pain, oral ulcer, post-op review — can wait until higher priority patients reviewed.

sections.heading: Neuro: reduced GCS, focal neurology with facial injury
items:
DCT Checklist: Before Ending Any Referral
□ Do I understand why OMFS has been asked to review?
□ Is the airway safe?
□ How urgent is this?
□ Have I informed my registrar if necessary?
□ Does the patient require admission?
□ Have I documented the referral?

sections.heading: Every referral deserves courtesy, even if ultimately inappropriate
items: Clarify the clinical question before attending. "Please review" is not a diagnosis

sections.heading: Repeat observations yourself if the patient appears unwell
items: If you think the referral is inappropriate, discuss professionally and explain reasoning. Never dismiss concerns without assessment

sections.heading: Airway, haemorrhage and sepsis take precedence over all other referrals
items: Good communication with referrers and seniors improves patient safety and workflow

sections.heading: Structured approach makes on-call safer, more efficient, less stressful
items:
Registrar Handover Prompt
Use SBAR. Situation: age, sex, location, presenting problem. Background: relevant PMH. Assessment: history, exam, obs, imaging. Recommendation: "I think..." "I'd like...". Before calling know: airway status, NEWS2, source tooth if swelling, mouth opening, dysphagia, bloods, imaging, working diagnosis, proposed plan.

title: Documentation, Clinical Notes and Medico-Legal Essentials
quote: Good clinicians make good decisions. Great clinicians make good decisions and document them well.

items:
Why This Matters
Documentation is a fundamental clinical skill. Every patient you assess, every procedure you perform, every referral you receive and every discussion you have with a senior colleague should be documented accurately. Your notes communicate with the MDT, provide a contemporaneous record, demonstrate clinical reasoning, support continuity of care, and form an important medico-legal document. Poor documentation places patients at risk. Excellent documentation protects patients, supports colleagues and reflects good clinical practice.

sections.heading: Golden Rule
items: If it is not documented, it is difficult to demonstrate that it happened.

sections.heading: Core Content
items:
Principles of Good Documentation
Every clinical entry should be: accurate, objective, legible, contemporaneous, dated, timed, signed, attributable to you.

Before You Start Writing
Ask yourself: What is the clinical problem? What have I found? What am I worried about? What have I done? What happens next? If your notes answer those five questions, they are likely to be useful.

Every Clinical Entry Should Include
Patient Details: name, hospital/NHS number, DOB
Date and Time: every entry must include both. Never add retrospectively without stating it.
Your Identification: full name, grade, signature or authenticated electronic signature

Structured Clinical Note
Presenting Complaint: "Referred from ED with increasing left facial swelling and trismus."
History: duration, progression, associated symptoms, previous treatment, relevant PMH. Document important negatives: "No dysphagia, no voice change, no difficulty breathing."
Examination: NEWS2, temperature, general appearance. Extraoral: swelling, tenderness, cellulitis, cranial nerves. Intraoral: source tooth, mouth opening mm, floor of mouth, occlusion, soft tissues.
Investigations: FBC, CRP, U&Es. Imaging: "Contrast CT neck demonstrates 2.5 cm left submandibular collection with surrounding cellulitis. Airway remains patent."
Impression: "Odontogenic infection arising from LL7 involving left submandibular space without current airway compromise."
Plan: Numbered. 1. Admit under OMFS, 2. IV antibiotics per local guideline, 3. Repeat airway assessment, 4. Contrast CT reviewed, 5. Discuss with registrar, 6. Theatre for I&D if indicated.

Documenting Discussions
Whenever you discuss with a senior, document: name of senior, time, advice received, agreed plan. Example: "Discussed with Mr Smith, Consultant OMFS, 18:40. Agreed admission, IV antibiotics, overnight airway observation, list for theatre tomorrow." Never write: "Consultant aware."

Telephone Referrals
Document: time, referrer name/designation/department, clinical question, advice given, planned review. Example: "21:15 – Telephone referral from Dr Patel, ED Reg. 32M with mandibular trauma post-assault. Advice: CT facial bones, soft diet, OMFS review. Patient to be assessed in ED."

Procedure Notes
Document: indication, consent, anaesthesia, procedure performed, findings, complications, outcome, post-op instructions, follow-up. Example: "Extraction LL8 under LA. Written informed consent. Time-out completed. IAN + long buccal blocks 2.2ml 2% lidocaine 1:80,000 adrenaline. LL8 elevated and delivered without complication. Socket curetted, irrigated saline. Haemostasis achieved. PO instructions given verbally and written. Patient discharged with analgesia and follow-up."

Relevant Negative Findings
Documenting important negatives shows you actively assessed for serious pathology. Facial swelling: no dysphagia, no stridor, no floor of mouth elevation, no voice change. Trauma: no malocclusion, no diplopia, no infraorbital paraesthesia, no CSF rhinorrhoea. Oral lesion: no induration, no cervical lymphadenopathy, no weight loss.

Writing Good Management Plans
Avoid: "Continue treatment." Write: 1. Repeat obs Q4H, 2. Continue IV antibiotics per guideline, 3. Soft diet, 4. Consultant review AM, 5. Repeat CRP AM, 6. Escalate immediately if airway symptoms develop. Specific plans improve safety.

Red Flags ⚠️
Documentation errors: no date/time, missing observations, no airway assessment, no working diagnosis, no management plan, no senior discussion, copying previous entries without confirming, unexplained abbreviations, recording assumptions as facts.

DCT Documentation Checklist
Before leaving the patient, confirm documented: □ Date and time, □ Presenting complaint, □ Relevant history, □ Observations, □ Examination findings, □ Relevant negatives, □ Investigation results, □ Working diagnosis, □ Numbered management plan, □ Senior discussion, □ Safety-netting, □ Your name and grade

sections.heading: If something worries you, document it and act on it
items: The quality of your notes is often a reflection of the quality of your assessment
Clear, concise notes make ward rounds, handovers and overnight reviews significantly easier

sections.heading: Document discussions with seniors in sufficient detail
items: Good documentation is an essential clinical skill and integral part of safe patient care

Registrar Handover Prompt
When presenting notes, ensure they answer: clinical problem, findings, worries, actions taken, next steps. If notes are clear, verbal handover will be clear.

title: Presenting Patients to the Registrar and Consultant
quote: A clear presentation is a clinical skill. It demonstrates organisation, prioritisation and sound clinical reasoning.

items:
Why This Matters
Every DCT will present patients to a registrar or consultant multiple times during every on-call shift. A concise, structured presentation enables rapid decision-making, improves patient safety and demonstrates professionalism. Your aim is not simply to relay information—you should interpret it, formulate a working diagnosis and propose an initial management plan. Senior clinicians do not expect perfection. They expect you to have assessed the patient, recognised the important findings and communicated them clearly.

sections.heading: Golden Rule
items: Never phone your registrar until you know what you are asking. Before making the call, ask yourself: Am I asking for advice? Am I requesting a review? Do I think the patient needs admission? Do I think the patient needs theatre?

sections.heading: Core Content
items:
Before You Pick Up the Phone
Ensure you know: patient name, hospital number, age, location, relevant medical history, observations/NEWS2, presenting complaint, key examination findings, blood results, imaging findings, working diagnosis, initial management, your recommendation. If you cannot answer these, review the patient again.

sections.heading: The One-Minute Presentation
items: Identify the Patient: "Hello, it's Dr Jones, the OMFS DCT. I'm calling about a 42-year-old gentleman in ED Majors."
Presenting Problem: "He has a two-day history of worsening left facial swelling associated with LL7." One sentence.
Relevant Background: Only include information that changes management: diabetes, anticoagulation, immunosuppression, previous radiotherapy, significant allergies.

Your Assessment: General condition, observations, airway, key exam findings. "NEWS2 is 2. Temperature 38.3°C. Airway is patent with no stridor or voice change. Left submandibular swelling, trismus 18mm, grossly carious LL7."
Investigations: Summarise important findings. "CRP is 165, WCC 17.4. CT demonstrates left submandibular collection without significant airway compression."
Your Impression: "I think this is a left submandibular space infection of odontogenic origin."
Your Plan: Finish with recommendation. "I'd like to admit him, commence IV antibiotics and discuss operative drainage."

The Consultant Wants to Know
Every senior will mentally ask: Is the patient sick? Is the airway safe? What is the diagnosis? Does the patient need admission? Does the patient need surgery? What have you already done? Answer these six questions.

Red Flags ⚠️
Escalate immediately if: airway compromise, significant haemorrhage, sepsis, deep neck infection, visual loss/diplopia after trauma, orbital compartment syndrome, rapidly deteriorating patient, any uncertainty regarding management.

DCT Checklist: Before Calling
□ Patient age and location
□ Mechanism or presenting complaint
□ Observations and NEWS2
□ Airway status
□ Examination findings
□ Imaging findings
□ Blood results
□ Working diagnosis
□ Your proposed plan

sections.heading: Registrars are assessing your clinical reasoning, not your memory
items: A concise one-minute presentation is more effective than a five-minute monologue

sections.heading: Key Takeaways
items: Structure every presentation the same way — situation, background, assessment, recommendation

sections.heading: Lead with the diagnosis and clinical status — not the chronology
items: Always include observations and airway assessment — seniors need to know if the patient is stable

sections.heading: Clear communication improves safety and builds confidence as an OMFS clinician
items:
Registrar Handover Prompt
Use SBAR. Situation: patient details + problem. Background: relevant PMH. Assessment: history, exam, obs, imaging. Recommendation: "I think..." "I'd like...". Be ready to answer: What worries you most? What do you want me to do?

title: Safe Handover in OMFS
quote: The quality of your handover is often the quality of your patient's overnight care.

items:
Why This Matters
Handover is one of the highest-risk moments in healthcare. Critical information can be lost, assumptions can be made and important tasks may be overlooked. Many serious incidents are linked not to poor clinical care, but to poor communication during transitions between teams. A safe handover ensures the incoming team understands who the patients are, why they are under OMFS, who is clinically unwell, what has been done, what still needs to happen, and what they should be concerned about overnight. Your responsibility does not end when your shift finishes—it ends when care has been safely transferred.

sections.heading: Golden Rule
items: Never hand over a task that you could reasonably complete before the end of your shift. Outstanding jobs should be the exception, not the rule.

sections.heading: A Structured Handover: I-PASS
items:
Prioritising Patients at Handover
Priority 1 – Immediate Attention: Airway compromise, active haemorrhage, septic patient, post-op deterioration, expanding neck swelling. Discuss first.
Priority 2 – Requires Review Overnight: Awaiting CT, repeat bloods, drain monitoring, facial swelling reassessment, post-op review.
Priority 3 – Routine Tasks: Discharge paperwork, prescriptions, clinic bookings, follow-up. Only hand over if genuinely unavoidable.

What Must Never Be Omitted
For every patient: working diagnosis, current observations, airway status, recent deterioration, pending investigations, outstanding treatment, senior involvement, escalation plan. If discussed with registrar/consultant, say so.

Red Flags ⚠️
Never leave without discussing: actual/potential airway compromise, active bleeding or high bleeding risk, septic or deteriorating, awaiting emergency surgery or returned from emergency theatre, unresolved diagnostic uncertainty requiring overnight reassessment.

DCT Handover Checklist
Before leaving shift, ensure incoming doctor knows: □ Patient name and location, □ Working diagnosis, □ Current clinical status, □ Airway assessment, □ Outstanding investigations, □ Outstanding tasks, □ Senior discussions, □ Escalation plan, □ Patients requiring overnight review, □ Patients expected back from theatre

sections.heading: Clearly distinguish between essential tasks and those that can wait
items: Highlight trends rather than isolated results — rising CRP or worsening trismus matters

sections.heading: Prioritise clinically unstable patients first — they get discussed first
items: Clearly communicate outstanding tasks, anticipated problems and escalation plans

sections.heading: Never leave until confident responsibility has been safely handed over
items:
Registrar Handover Prompt
When giving handover, start with sickest patients. For each: one-line summary, current status, specific jobs, specific triggers for escalation: "Please review immediately if mouth opening deteriorates below 15mm or new dysphagia develops."

title: Surviving the Ward Round
quote: The best ward rounds are organised before they begin. Preparation saves time, improves patient care and allows the team to focus on clinical decision-making rather than administration.

items:
Why This Matters
The ward round is the centrepiece of inpatient care in OMFS. It is where diagnoses are reviewed, treatment plans refined, patients prepared for theatre, discharge decisions made and complications recognised. For a new DCT, ward rounds can feel intimidating. They are often fast-paced, involve multiple disciplines and require you to think, document and organise simultaneously. Your role is not simply to write notes—it is to ensure every decision made is translated into safe, effective patient care. The most successful DCTs are not those with the greatest clinical knowledge; they are the ones who are organised, anticipate what the team needs and ensure nothing is forgotten.

sections.heading: Golden Rule
items: Preparation before the ward round saves time afterwards. A consultant should spend their time making clinical decisions—not waiting for blood results to be found or scans to be opened.

sections.heading: Core Content
items:
Before the Ward Round
Arrive early. Before consultant arrives: □ Review every patient, □ Read overnight handover, □ Check nursing concerns, □ Review overnight obs, □ Check NEWS2, □ Review blood results, □ Review microbiology, □ Open all relevant imaging, □ Check theatre lists, □ Identify planned discharges, □ Speak to nurse in charge. If something changed overnight, know about it before you’re asked.

Organising Your Patient List
For each patient include: name, age, hospital number, location, diagnosis, admission date, operations performed, outstanding investigations, expected discharge date. Leave space for today's plan.

The Consultant Will Usually Ask
For every inpatient: Why are they in hospital? Which operation have they had? How many days post-op? How were they overnight? What do today's bloods show? Have they eaten and mobilised? Are they fit for discharge? What still needs to happen?

Presenting an Inpatient
Concise presentation <30 seconds: "Mr Brown is a 62-year-old, day one following I&D of left submandibular abscess with extraction LL7. Overnight afebrile, NEWS2 1, pain controlled, tolerating oral fluids. CRP fallen 186 to 112. Drain output minimal. Remains on IV antibiotics."

Writing the Ward Round Entry
Include: date and time, consultant leading, current clinical status, examination findings, investigation results, assessment, numbered management plan, your name and designation. Example:
Consultant Ward Round – Mr Smith – 08:15
Day 2 post ORIF left mandibular angle. Comfortable at rest. Afebrile. NEWS2 0. Wounds clean. Occlusion stable. Mild lower lip paraesthesia unchanged. Bloods improving.
Plan
1. Continue IV co-amoxiclav today
2. Convert to oral antibiotics tomorrow if appropriate
3. Soft diet 6 weeks
4. Physio jaw exercises
5. Repeat FBC/CRP tomorrow
6. Home tomorrow if well

The Ward Jobs List
Prioritise by urgency:
Priority 1 – Immediate: Deteriorating patient, blood transfusion, theatre consent, CT request, urgent senior review, airway concerns.
Priority 2 – Time-Critical: Prescriptions, blood requests, drain removal, micro discussion, referrals.
Priority 3 – Routine: Discharge summaries, follow-up appointments, clinic letters, updating list.

Red Flags ⚠️
Never ignore: increasing NEWS2, new dysphagia, voice change, increasing swelling, bleeding, reduced urine output, confusion, increasing O2 requirement. Escalate concerns early.

DCT Ward Round Checklist
Before leaving each patient: □ Today's exam documented? □ Consultant's plan written clearly? □ Jobs added to list? □ Nursing team know the plan? □ Outstanding investigations? □ For theatre? □ Suitable for discharge?

sections.heading: Good organisation is a defining characteristic of an excellent OMFS DCT
items:
Registrar Handover Prompt
After ward round, summarise for your registrar: sick patients first, new plans, new admissions, expected discharges, theatre list changes, any concerns. Use the same structure as your jobs list.

title: Theatre Survival for the OMFS DCT
quote: Theatre is not just where operations happen—it is where surgeons are trained. Preparation, anticipation and teamwork are as important as technical skill.

items:
Why This Matters
For many new DCTs, theatre is an unfamiliar environment with its own language, routines, etiquette and expectations. It can feel intimidating, but it is also where some of the most valuable learning in OMFS takes place. A good assistant makes every operation safer, more efficient and more enjoyable. Your role is not passive—you are an integral part of the surgical team. By understanding the procedure, anticipating the next step and maintaining situational awareness, you contribute directly to patient safety and your own surgical development.

sections.heading: Golden Rule
items: The best assistant is the one the surgeon hardly has to ask. Anticipation, preparation and communication are the hallmarks of an excellent theatre assistant.

sections.heading: Core Content
items:
Before the Theatre List
Review: operating list, indication for each procedure, relevant imaging, clinic letters, bloods, consent forms. Ask: Why is this operation being performed? What anatomy is at risk? What complications might occur? What instruments are likely to be required? 15 minutes reading the evening before improves learning more than reading afterwards.

Arriving in Theatre
Aim to arrive before the consultant. Introduce yourself to: theatre nurses, ODPs, anaesthetists, recovery staff, students. Learn names. Good teamwork starts with communication.

Your Responsibilities Before First Patient
Check: □ Operating list correct, □ Imaging available, □ Consent completed, □ Notes present, □ Bloods available, □ Implants/equipment available, □ You understand the procedure.

Understanding the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist
Sign In — before anaesthesia: patient ID, procedure, consent, allergies, airway, antibiotics, anticipated risks.
Time Out — before incision: correct patient/procedure/site, team introductions, imaging, equipment, critical steps. Every team member can speak up.
Sign Out — before patient leaves: procedure performed, counts correct, specimens labelled, equipment issues, post-op plan.

Scrubbing, Gowning and Gloving
Maintain strict aseptic technique. Remove jewellery, nails short/no varnish, surgical hand prep per local policy, hands above elbows after scrubbing, avoid non-sterile surfaces. If sterility broken, inform team and re-scrub. Patient safety before embarrassment.

How to Be an Excellent Assistant
Good assistants: hold retractors steadily, maintain tissue tension, keep field visible, suction without obstructing, follow the operation, anticipate next instrument, protect soft tissues. Poor assistance makes simple procedures difficult.

Anticipating the Operation
For surgical extraction: LA → incision → flap → bone removal → tooth sectioning → delivery → debridement → irrigation → haemostasis → closure. Understanding sequence lets you anticipate instruments and improve flow.

Common OMFS Theatre Procedures
During DCT year you’ll likely assist: surgical removal of impacted teeth, I&D of odontogenic infections, ORIF facial fractures, dentoalveolar trauma, soft tissue biopsies, excision of oral lesions, neck dissections, skin lesion excisions, salivary gland surgery, tracheostomy.

After the Operation
Before leaving theatre ensure: operation note completed, drug chart updated, post-op instructions documented, specimens sent, imaging reviewed if required, relatives updated, follow-up arranged. Never assume someone else has completed these.

Red Flags ⚠️
In theatre: unlabelled specimen, missing swab/instrument, patient moved before Time Out, allergy not checked, wrong site marking, sterility breach not declared. Speak up — it’s your responsibility.

DCT Theatre Checklist
Before list: □ Read about procedures, □ Review imaging, □ Check consent, □ Know diagnosis, □ Understand operation.
During: □ Maintain sterility, □ Retract effectively, □ Anticipate instruments, □ Protect tissues, □ Observe anatomy.
After: □ Documentation complete, □ Post-op plan confirmed, □ Follow-up arranged, □ Reflect on learning.

sections.heading: Respect tissues, maintain sterility, communicate with the team
items: Every operation is an opportunity to improve technical knowledge, anatomy, and judgement

Registrar Handover Prompt
After theatre, update your registrar: cases done, complications, drains, antibiotics, post-op instructions, concerns, plans for review. Be specific: “Patient returned to ward, obs stable, drain 20ml, plan review AM with consultant.”

title: Looking After Yourself on Call
quote: You cannot provide safe care for patients if you do not look after yourself. Fatigue, hunger, stress and poor organisation affect clinical performance more than most trainees realise.

items:
Why This Matters
Every OMFS DCT remembers their first on-call shift. It can be exciting, rewarding, exhausting and, at times, overwhelming. You will assess patients in pain, deal with emergencies at night, make important clinical decisions and manage competing priorities. No one expects you to know everything. What is expected is that you remain organised, recognise your limitations, ask for help when appropriate and continue to provide safe, compassionate care. Looking after yourself is not a luxury—it is a professional responsibility. A tired, dehydrated and stressed clinician is more likely to make mistakes.

sections.heading: Golden Rule
items: Your first responsibility is to keep patients safe. Your second responsibility is to keep yourself fit to do that. There is no benefit in "soldiering on" if you are exhausted, unwell or struggling.

sections.heading: Core Content
items:
Before Your Shift
Evening before: check rota, know location, know on-call consultant/registrar, check expected theatre lists, get adequate sleep.
On the day: eat a proper meal, bring water bottle, healthy snacks, charger, notebook, pens, ensure hospital system access works. Starting a 12-hour shift hungry is rarely a good idea.

Organise Yourself Early
Within first 30 minutes: □ Introduce yourself to nursing teams, □ Meet registrar, □ Know how to contact consultant, □ Find emergency theatre, □ Locate OMFS ward, □ Check emergency airway equipment location, □ Understand referral pathways. Familiarity reduces stress in emergencies.

Managing Multiple Jobs
Ask: "Which patient is at greatest risk if I delay?" Prioritise by clinical urgency, not bleep order. Airway always takes priority over paperwork.

sections.heading: The Four Categories of Work
items: Immediate: Airway compromise, active haemorrhage, septic patient, rapid deterioration, emergency theatre
Urgent: Facial cellulitis, mandibular fracture, facial laceration, dental trauma, review after CT

sections.heading: Routine: Dental pain, dry socket, ward jobs, routine reviews
items: Administrative: Discharge summaries, clinic letters, filing, updating lists. Complete when clinical work allows.

Looking After Your Basic Needs
During busy shift: drink water regularly, eat when you can, toilet before desperate, sit for a few minutes if safe. Small breaks improve concentration and reduce errors.

Fatigue
Affects decision-making, memory, communication, technical skills, professionalism. If re-reading notes, forgetting tasks, unusually irritable, struggling to concentrate: pause, hydrate, eat if possible, ask for support.

When to Call Your Registrar
Call early if: worried about airway, patient deteriorating, think emergency surgery needed, significant bleeding, unsure of diagnosis, feel out of depth. Registrar would rather be called early than after preventable deterioration.

Red Flags ⚠️
Personal red flags: making simple mistakes, forgetting to document, snapping at colleagues, feeling unsafe to drive home, dreading next shift. These signal you need support — speak to ES, TPD, or colleague.

DCT On-Call Checklist
Before every shift: □ Have I eaten? □ Do I have water? □ Do I know who my registrar is? □ Is my bleep working? □ Do I know where emergency theatre is? □ Do I have a notebook? □ Do I know how to contact consultant?

At the End of Your Shift
Before leaving: □ Complete urgent jobs, □ Handover outstanding tasks clearly, □ Ensure sick patients discussed, □ Check documentation, □ Return borrowed equipment, □ Thank the team. Leave work at work. Recovery between shifts is important.

sections.heading: Looking after yourself is a professional responsibility, not a luxury
items: Your career is a marathon — sleep, exercise, hobbies, family/friends sustain you

Registrar Handover Prompt
When asking for help because you’re overwhelmed: be honest. “I’m managing three referrals, one is airway risk, I’ve seen him but not started the others. Can you advise priority or come to help?” Specific requests get specific support.
Batch complete: Modules 6–10 done.
Next up per your plan: Modules 11–15 (Facial Swelling, Ludwig’s Angina, Odontogenic Infection, Pericoronitis, Dry Socket).

title: Managing the Acutely Unwell OMFS Patient
quote: The first job of the OMFS DCT is not to know everything—it is to recognise the sick patient, provide safe initial management, and know when to ask for help.

items:
Why This Matters
Deterioration on OMFS wards is often due to airway compromise from facial swelling, sepsis from odontogenic infections, or post-operative bleeding. As the DCT, you’ll usually be first to review. Your job is not to diagnose every cause — it’s to recognise illness, start ABCDE, and escalate. Early escalation is good judgement, not weakness.

sections.heading: Golden Rule
items: Treat the patient, not the numbers. But never ignore the numbers. If NEWS2 ≥5, or you are worried, escalate. You can always de-escalate later.

sections.heading: 1. Recognising Deterioration: NEWS2 + OMFS Red Flags
items:
OMFS-specific red flags that trump NEWS2:
Stridor, drooling, new voice change, rapidly expanding neck swelling, saturations <92% on air, GCS drop ≥2, new proptosis/diplopia.

sections.heading: 3. The Big Three OMFS Emergencies
items:
A. Airway Compromise
Causes: Ludwig’s angina, post-op haematoma, angioedema, trauma.
Actions: O2, sit up 45°, nebulised adrenaline 5ml 1:1000 if stridor, call anaesthetics + OMFS reg +theatres. Do NOT lie flat. Do NOT attempt to examine throat if high risk.

B. Sepsis
Think Sepsis 6 within 1 hour: O2, blood cultures, lactate/VBG, IV antibiotics per local OMFSguidelines, IV fluids, urine output, senior review.
Common OMFS sources: odontogenic, necrotising fasciitis, aspiration pneumonia.

C. Haemorrhage
Post-op neck: remove skin clips, evacuate clot at bedside if airway threatened, call theatres.
Intra-oral: pressure, tranexamic acid 1g IV, packing. Activate major haemorrhage protocol if>150ml/min or haemodynamic instability.

sections.heading: New confusion in elderly = hypoxia, sepsis, or bleed until proven otherwise
items:
DCT Checklist: Deteriorating Patient
□ A: Airway patent? Adjuncts needed?
□ B: RR, SpO2, O2 on?
□ C: HR, BP, IV access, fluids running?
□ D: GCS, glucose checked?
□ E: Temp, exposed surgical site?
□ NEWS2 calculated and handed over
□ Bloods: FBC, U&E, CRP, lactate, clotting, G&S
□ ECG if tachycardia/chest pain
□ Seniors informed: who, when, what said
□ Documentation timed and signed

sections.heading: If you’re worried at the bedside, you’re already late. Worried = escalate
items: “Patient stable for now” is a dangerous phrase in facial swelling — document time of nextplanned review
In post-op neck haematoma, opening the wound at the bedside can be life-saving. If in doubt,cut the sutures
Lactate >2 in OMFS infection = assume deep neck space involvement until proven otherwise

sections.heading: Key Takeaways
items: NEWS2 + OMFS red flags — use both. A score of 4 with stridor still needs anaesthetics now
ABCDE + call for help — you can do both simultaneously. Never assess alone if worried
Airway, sepsis, bleeding — the three OMFS killers. Know the immediate steps for each
SBAR when you escalate — Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation. Be clear
Document times — when you noticed, when you called, who you spoke to, what plan was made

Registrar Handover Prompt - SBAR
Before calling, structure it:
S: “I’m calling about Mr Smith, a 45yo day-1 post-op neck dissection, NEWS 8”
B: “He was fine 1hr ago, now stridor and neck swelling since drain removed”
A: “I think he has a post-op haematoma compromising airway. RR 28, SpO2 91% on 15L”
R: “I need you to come now and I’ve called anaesthetics. Shall I open the wound?”
Here’s Module 12 standardised per your plan. Modules 13–16 will follow next.

sections.heading: "Always assess the airway before the tooth."
items:
Why This Matters
Facial swelling is the commonest emergency presentation seen by OMFS teams and one of the first conditions every Dental Core Trainee must learn to manage confidently. Although many patients have relatively localised odontogenic infections that can be treated safely with drainage and elimination of the source, a small proportion will develop rapidly progressive infections involving the deep fascial spaces of the head and neck. These infections can threaten the airway, spread into the mediastinum, result in overwhelming sepsis and, if untreated, become life-threatening. The challenge is not simply diagnosing an abscess — it is identifying the patient who is becoming critically unwell. Your priorities: assess the airway, recognise sepsis, identify the source, decide whether source control is required, escalate early.

sections.heading: Golden Rule
items: Always assess the airway before the tooth. Never become distracted by dental findings while overlooking a threatened airway.

sections.heading: Core Content
items:
BEFORE YOU PHONE YOUR REGISTRAR
Know: □ Is airway patent? □ Can patient speak in full sentences? □ Dysphagia? □ Odynophagia? □ Voice change? □ Drooling? □ Stridor? □ Maximum mouth opening (mm)? □ Which tooth is responsible? □ Is floor of mouth elevated? □ Temperature? □ NEWS2? □ CRP? □ WCC? □ Has CT been performed? □ Does patient need admission? If you cannot answer, reassess before calling.

The First Five Minutes – ABCDE
Airway: First priority. Look for stridor, difficulty speaking, difficulty swallowing saliva, drooling, “hot potato” voice, tongue elevation, floor of mouth swelling, respiratory distress. Ask: “Are you finding it difficult to breathe?” “Can you swallow your saliva?” If any concern: stay with patient, call registrar immediately, inform ED senior, involve anaesthetics early. Do NOT send unstable patient to CT before senior review.
Breathing: RR, SpO2, work of breathing, chest expansion, O2 requirement.
Circulation: HR, BP, CRT, perfusion. Look for sepsis.
Disability: Conscious level AVPU/GCS, confusion, glucose if appropriate.
Exposure: Extent of swelling, cellulitis, skin erythema, surgical scars, draining sinuses. Check temperature.

History
Presenting Complaint: Patient’s own words. “Left facial swelling for three days.”
HPC: Onset: sudden/gradual? Progression: improving/worsening/fluctuating? Rapid progression concerning. Pain: SOCRATES. Dental symptoms: toothache, broken tooth, recent extraction, previous swelling, previous antibiotics, RCT?
Red Flag Symptoms: Always ask specifically: difficulty swallowing, difficulty breathing, voice change, drooling, neck swelling, reduced mouth opening, fever, rigors.
Medical History: Diabetes, steroids, chemo, immunosuppression, previous H&N radiotherapy, bisphosphonates/denosumab, cardiac, pregnancy. Poorly controlled diabetes significantly increases risk.

Examination
General: Appearance, NEWS2, temperature, pulse, BP, RR, SpO2, hydration, distress.
Extraoral: Site, facial asymmetry, swelling, skin erythema, bruising, surgical scars. Palpate: tenderness, fluctuance, induration, crepitus, cervical nodes, mandibular border, salivary glands.
Mouth Opening: Always measure inter-incisal distance. Normal 35–50mm. <20mm significant trismus. Progressive trismus often indicates spread into muscles of mastication or adjacent spaces.
Intraoral: OH, carious teeth, pericoronitis, vestibular swelling, palatal swelling, floor of mouth, tongue position, pus discharge, tooth mobility, sinus tracts. Identify likely source.

sections.heading: Which Fascial Space Is Involved?
items:
Red Flags 🚩
Escalate immediately if: stridor, difficulty managing secretions, voice change, tongue elevation, raised floor of mouth, bilateral submandibular swelling, rapidly progressive swelling, trismus <20mm, sepsis, immunocompromised, failure to improve despite antibiotics, nursing/ED concern that patient deteriorating.

Investigations
Bloods: FBC, CRP, U&E, blood cultures if febrile/septic, VBG with lactate if systemically unwell, G&S if surgery anticipated. Remember: blood tests support assessment — they do not replace it.
OPG: Identify source tooth, impacted teeth, periapical pathology. Does not define extent of deep neck infection.
Contrast-Enhanced CT Neck: Investigation of choice when: deep space infection suspected, significant neck swelling, source uncertain, trismus/dysphagia/systemic toxicity, surgical drainage considered. Helps distinguish cellulitis from drainable abscess and defines extent.

sections.heading: Management Algorithm
items: ABCDE. Is airway threatened? Yes → Call registrar, anaesthetics, ED senior immediately. Prepare for definitive airway. No → Continue.

sections.heading: Establish source: Odontogenic, salivary, non-odontogenic?
items: Deep fascial space infection? Yes → Contrast CT if safe + discuss urgently with reg. No → Assess for localised infection.
Source control: Extraction of causative tooth where appropriate. I&D of drainable collection. Remember: antibiotics are adjunct, not substitute for source control.

Admission Criteria
Consider if: airway concerns, deep fascial space infection, significant trismus, dysphagia/odynophagia, requirement for IV antibiotics, requirement for surgical drainage, sepsis, significant comorbidities, failure of outpatient treatment, inadequate social support.

Indications for Surgery
Consider when: drainable abscess, failure of medical management, progressive infection, clear odontogenic source requiring removal, deep fascial space involvement. Objectives: eliminate source, drain pus, decompress infected spaces, obtain microbiology.

Antibiotics
Support definitive treatment. Choose per local antimicrobial guidelines, allergy status, severity, route. Never rely on antibiotics alone when source control required.

Discharge Criteria
Suitable if: no airway concerns, systemically well, localised infection, can tolerate oral intake, definitive treatment done or clear plan, follow-up arranged, understands safety-netting. Advise return if swelling progresses, swallowing difficult, or breathing changes.

DCT Checklist: Before You Phone Your Registrar
□ Airway status
□ NEWS2
□ Maximum mouth opening
□ Source tooth
□ Floor of mouth findings
□ Dysphagia or voice change
□ Blood results
□ Imaging findings
□ Working diagnosis
□ Whether admission/surgery required

sections.heading: If worried, escalate early — senior review should never be delayed
items:
Registrar Handover Prompt
SBAR: Situation — age, sex, location, problem. Background — PMH. Assessment — history, exam, obs, imaging. Recommendation — “I think... I'd like...”. Know: airway, NEWS2, mouth opening, source, floor of mouth, dysphagia, bloods, CT, working diagnosis, plan.

sections.heading: "Ludwig's angina is an airway emergency until proven otherwise."
items:
Why This Matters
Ludwig's angina is one of the few true life-threatening emergencies in OMFS. It is a rapidly spreading cellulitis involving bilateral submandibular, sublingual and submental spaces. Oedema, rather than pus, causes early airway compromise as the tongue is displaced superiorly and posteriorly. Mortality was historically >50%. Modern management has improved outcomes, but delay kills. Your priorities: protect the airway, recognise sepsis, start treatment, escalate early, achieve source control.

sections.heading: Golden Rule
items: If you think it might be Ludwig's angina, treat it as an airway emergency until proven otherwise. Never be falsely reassured by a patient who is still talking.

sections.heading: Core Content
items:
What Is Ludwig's Angina?
Rapidly progressive cellulitis, usually odontogenic from mandibular molars. Involves submandibular, sublingual, submental spaces bilaterally. Early problem is diffuse inflammatory oedema causing airway compression.

Initial Assessment – ABCDE
A - Airway: Stridor, voice change “hot potato”, drooling, inability to swallow saliva, tongue elevation, floor of mouth swelling, respiratory distress. Ask: “Can you swallow your saliva?” If no, escalate immediately. Do NOT repeatedly examine mouth if airway compromised.
B - Breathing: RR, SpO2, accessory muscle use. O2 if indicated.
C - Circulation: HR, BP, CRT, temp. Look for sepsis.
D - Disability: GCS, confusion, glucose.
E - Exposure: Bilateral submandibular swelling, diffuse neck swelling, warmth, woody induration. Neck often firm, not fluctuant.

Red Flags ⚠️
Immediate senior review if: stridor, drooling, difficulty swallowing saliva, voice change, tongue elevation, bilateral submandibular swelling, raised floor of mouth, rapid deterioration, respiratory distress, sepsis, reduced GCS. One red flag justifies escalation.

DCT Checklist: Before You Phone Your Registrar
□ Is airway patent?
□ Can patient swallow saliva?
□ Stridor?
□ Voice change?
□ Tongue elevated?
□ Floor of mouth raised and indurated?
□ Swelling bilateral?
□ Patient septic?
□ NEWS2?
□ Observations?
□ Anaesthetic team informed?
□ Senior ED review?
□ CT performed or unsafe to send?

sections.heading: Initial Management
items: ABCDE. Call registrar, consultant, anaesthetics, senior ED clinician. Early multidisciplinary involvement saves lives.
Move to resus area. Continuous monitoring. Do not leave unattended.
IV access x2. Bloods: FBC, CRP, U&E, blood cultures, VBG with lactate, G&S.
IV fluids if indicated.
IV antibiotics per local guidelines — broad spectrum with anaerobic cover.

Assess need for definitive airway. Options: awake fibre-optic intubation, video-assisted intubation, surgical airway. Decision by anaesthetics + OMFS senior. Never attempt advanced airway beyond competence.
Do not delay airway management for CT. Unstable patient belongs in resus/theatre.

Investigations
Contrast-Enhanced CT Neck: Defines extent, abscess vs cellulitis, airway deviation, mediastinal spread. But do not delay airway management to obtain it.

Definitive Surgical Management
Once airway secure: remove source tooth, incise and drain involved spaces if indicated, obtain microbiology, irrigate, place drains. Not every patient has mature abscess — decompression may still be required.

sections.heading: Definitive management: airway protection, antibiotics, source control
items:
Registrar Handover Prompt
SBAR: “32M in ED with Ludwig’s angina. Stridor, unable to swallow saliva, tongue elevated, NEWS 7. I’m concerned about airway. Anaesthetics en route. Need you now. Shall we prepare for theatre?”

title: Odontogenic Infection
quote: Most odontogenic infections are straightforward. The skill lies in recognising the few that are not.

items:
Why This Matters
Odontogenic infection is the commonest reason for emergency OMFS referral. Most are uncomplicated and managed with drainage + source control. A small number progress rapidly through fascial planes, causing sepsis, airway compromise, and death. Your job: assess airway, recognise sepsis, identify source, decide if source control needed, escalate early. A swollen face is not the diagnosis — it’s the symptom.

sections.heading: Golden Rule
items: Pus needs a scalpel, not just a prescription pad. Antibiotics support treatment. They rarely replace definitive source control.

sections.heading: Core Content
items:
Pathophysiology
Starts with pulpal necrosis → periapical spread → perforates bone → spreads via path of least resistance. Root apex position vs muscle attachments determines fascial space involved.

Initial Assessment – ABCDE
Most have normal airway, but never assume. Specifically assess: difficulty swallowing, voice change, floor of mouth swelling, bilateral neck swelling, respiratory distress. These suggest progression beyond simple infection.

History
Onset: Hours, days, weeks? Rapid progression concerning.
Pain: Severity, constant/intermittent, worse on biting, night pain.
Dental symptoms: Toothache, broken tooth, recent extraction, pericoronitis.
Red flags: Dysphagia, odynophagia, voice change, drooling, fever, rigors, trismus.
PMH: Diabetes, steroids, chemo, immunosuppression, radiotherapy, MRONJ risk, pregnancy.

Examination
General: Temp, pulse, BP, RR, SpO2, NEWS2. Septic appearance?
Extraoral: Site/extent of swelling, skin erythema, tenderness, fluctuance, induration, cervical lymph nodes.
Mouth opening: Measure inter-incisal distance. Normal 35–50mm. <20mm = significant trismus.
Intraoral: Oral hygiene, carious teeth, tooth mobility, percussion tenderness, buccal/palatal swelling, floor of mouth, tongue position, pus discharge, sinus tracts. Identify source tooth.

sections.heading: Which Fascial Space?
items:
Red Flags ⚠️
Escalate immediately: stridor, difficulty managing secretions, voice change, tongue elevation, raised floor of mouth, bilateral submandibular swelling, rapidly progressive swelling, trismus <20mm, sepsis, immunocompromised, failure to improve on antibiotics, nursing/ED concern.

Investigations
Bloods: FBC, CRP, U&E, blood cultures if febrile/septic, VBG with lactate if unwell. Normal CRP does not exclude serious infection early.
OPG: Identify source tooth, impacted teeth, periapical pathology. Does not define extent of deep infection.
Contrast CT Neck: Investigation of choice if deep space infection suspected, significant neck swelling, uncertain source, trismus/dysphagia/toxicity, considering drainage. Answers: cellulitis vs abscess, extent.

sections.heading: Management Algorithm
items: ABCDE. Is airway threatened? Yes → call reg, anaesthetics, ED senior now.

sections.heading: Establish source: Odontogenic, salivary, non-odontogenic?
items: Deep fascial space? Yes → contrast CT if safe + urgent reg discussion.
Source control: Extraction, endo, I&D. Antibiotics are adjunct, not substitute.

Admission Criteria
Consider if: airway concerns, deep space infection, significant trismus, dysphagia, sepsis, IV antibiotics needed, surgery needed, significant comorbidity, failed outpatient treatment.

Antibiotics
Indicated when: spreading cellulitis, systemic involvement, drainage not immediately achievable, significant comorbidities, deep space infection. Not routinely required for every dental abscess if drainage + source control achieved in healthy patient. Follow local guidelines.

DCT Checklist: Before You Phone Your Registrar
□ Is airway normal?
□ Is patient systemically well?
□ Which tooth is responsible?
□ Is there trismus? Document mm.
□ Is there dysphagia?
□ Is there fluctuance?
□ Is there a collection needing drainage?
□ Does patient need IV antibiotics?
□ Does patient require admission?
□ Is imaging required?

sections.heading: When in doubt, reassess and escalate — deterioration can be rapid
items:
Registrar Handover Prompt
Know: airway status, NEWS2, source tooth, mouth opening, floor of mouth, dysphagia/voice change, bloods, CT findings, working diagnosis, whether source control achieved, admission need.

title: Pericoronitis
quote: Not every wisdom tooth infection needs admission—but every wisdom tooth infection deserves a careful assessment.

items:
Why This Matters
Pericoronitis is one of the commonest reasons for emergency dental and OMFS attendance. 80–90% involve mandibular third molars in young adults. Most episodes are mild and managed as outpatient with local measures. However, infection can spread beyond the operculum into fascial spaces, causing trismus, cellulitis, deep neck infection and airway compromise. The OMFS DCT must distinguish simple pericoronitis from spreading odontogenic infection.

sections.heading: Golden Rule
items: Treat the patient, not the wisdom tooth. The presence of an inflamed operculum is less important than the patient's airway, systemic condition and extent of infection.

sections.heading: Core Content
items:
What Is Pericoronitis?
Inflammation/infection of soft tissues around crown of partially erupted tooth. Most commonly mandibular thirds, 18–30 years. Food/plaque accumulates under operculum → anaerobic bacterial growth. Recurrent attacks common unless cause addressed.

Risk Factors
Partially erupted lower 8, poor OH, food stagnation, opposing upper 8 trauma, smoking, stress, recent URTI, pregnancy.

Initial Assessment – ABCDE
Diagnosis often obvious, but start with ABCDE. Assess airway: voice change, difficulty swallowing, floor of mouth swelling, respiratory distress. These are NOT typical of uncomplicated pericoronitis and suggest spreading infection.

History
Presenting complaint: Pain around wisdom tooth, swollen gum, difficulty chewing, bad taste, difficulty opening mouth.
HPC: Onset sudden/gradual? First episode or recurrent? Improving/worsening? Severity, radiation to ear, pain on biting, night pain. Functional: difficulty opening mouth, swallowing, reduced intake, speech changes.
Previous episodes: “Keeps happening every few months” = indication for definitive treatment.

Examination
General: Comfortable, in pain, septic? Temp, pulse, NEWS2.
Extraoral: Facial swelling, cervical lymphadenopathy, tenderness, trismus. Measure mouth opening.
Intraoral: Partially erupted tooth, inflamed operculum, pus, food debris, ulceration, opposing upper 8 trauma, oral hygiene. Palpate gently for tenderness/drainage.

Typical Clinical Features
Pain around partially erupted lower 8, inflamed operculum, halitosis, bad taste, local swelling, mild trismus, tender cervical nodes. These alone do not indicate severe infection.

Red Flags ⚠️
Escalate if: dysphagia, voice change, bilateral submandibular swelling, raised floor of mouth, significant facial swelling, mouth opening <20mm, sepsis, rapid progression, immunocompromised. Think beyond pericoronitis → spreading odontogenic infection.

Investigations
Bloods: Usually unnecessary in uncomplicated cases. Consider FBC, CRP, U&E if systemically unwell, admission likely, significant swelling, concern re spreading infection.
OPG: Investigation of choice. Assess tooth position, impaction, IAN relationship, caries, distal caries in 7, associated pathology.
CT: Rarely required. Indications: significant facial swelling, neck swelling, deep space infection, diagnostic uncertainty, abscess concern.

Management
Mild: Irrigation under operculum with saline/chlorhexidine, remove food debris, OHI, analgesia, warm saline rinses. Antibiotics NOT routinely indicated.
Moderate: Local debridement, OHI, analgesia, antibiotics only if spreading infection/systemic involvement per local guidelines.
Severe: Trismus, facial swelling, cellulitis, dysphagia, systemic illness → admit, IV antibiotics per guidelines, imaging if indicated, urgent reg discussion.

Should Tooth Be Extracted Acutely?
Exam question. In selected cases, extraction acutely is appropriate and provides immediate source control if access adequate and operator experienced. However, severe trismus, extensive cellulitis, limited access may make immediate extraction unsafe. Priority is controlling acute infection before definitive treatment. Decision individualised.

Definitive Management
Recurrent pericoronitis, repeated antibiotics, recurrent pain/swelling, caries/periodontal disease → assess for removal of 8 per NICE/accepted guidance.

Admission Criteria
Airway concerns, significant trismus, dysphagia, facial cellulitis, deep space infection, IV antibiotics needed, significant comorbidity, failed outpatient management.

DCT Checklist: Before You Phone Your Registrar
□ Which wisdom tooth?
□ Airway normal?
□ Trismus? Record mm.
□ Dysphagia/odynophagia?
□ Facial swelling?
□ Pus?
□ Systemically unwell?
□ Previous episodes?
□ Extraction likely required?
□ Admission needed?

sections.heading: Key Takeaways
items: Most pericoronitis is local inflammatory process, but exclude spreading infection first
Antibiotics only if systemic involvement/spreading cellulitis — local measures sufficient for many

sections.heading: Recurrent pericoronitis usually requires definitive management of offending 8
items: If dysphagia, significant trismus, or facial swelling develops, reassess urgently

Registrar Handover Prompt
Know: which tooth, airway status, mouth opening, facial swelling, pus, dysphagia, obs, OPG findings, whether admission needed.

title: Dry Socket (Alveolar Osteitis)
quote: A dry socket is intensely painful but almost never dangerous. Your role is to recognise it, exclude more serious pathology and provide effective pain relief and reassurance.

items:
Why This Matters
Dry socket is one of the commonest complications after dental extraction and a frequent reason for emergency attendance. Patients are often extremely distressed because pain can be severe, radiate widely, and appear disproportionate to clinical findings. The commonest mistake is prescribing antibiotics. Dry socket is not primarily an infection and antibiotics have little/no role in uncomplicated cases. Your role: confirm diagnosis, exclude other pathology, provide pain relief, reassure, promote healing.

sections.heading: Golden Rule
items: Severe pain with very little swelling is usually dry socket until proven otherwise.

sections.heading: Core Content
items:
What Is Dry Socket?
Alveolar osteitis occurs when normal blood clot in extraction socket is lost or breaks down prematurely. Without clot: alveolar bone exposed, nerve endings uncovered, healing delayed, severe pain develops. Importantly: no established suppurative infection in uncomplicated dry socket. This explains why antibiotics are generally ineffective.

Incidence
1–5% routine extractions. Up to 30% mandibular third molar surgical extractions. Highest after difficult lower 8s.

Risk Factors
Surgical extraction, mandibular thirds, smoking, previous dry socket, oral contraceptive use, difficult/traumatic extraction, poor OH, pre-existing infection, increasing age. Smoking is strongest modifiable risk factor.

Pathophysiology
Premature fibrinolysis destroys clot → socket empty → bone exposed → healing delayed → pain fibres directly stimulated. Pain often far greater than clinical appearance.

Initial Assessment – ABCDE
Not an emergency, but systematic assessment still required. Most have normal airway, breathing, circulation. Disability: pain may be severe despite normal exam. Exposure: look for facial swelling, cellulitis, bruising. Systemic abnormality should prompt reconsideration.

History
Timing: Most useful clue. Pain develops 2–5 days post-extraction. Immediate post-op pain less likely dry socket.
Pain: Severe, deep, constant, throbbing, radiating to ear/temple/neck, poorly relieved by simple analgesics.
Associated: Bad taste, halitosis, difficulty eating, facial swelling, fever, trismus. Swelling/fever uncommon in uncomplicated dry socket.

Examination
Extraoral: Usually normal. No significant swelling, cellulitis, neck swelling. Document obs.
Intraoral: Empty socket, partial clot loss, exposed bone, grey/yellow fibrin, food debris, local tenderness. Surrounding gingiva relatively healthy. Gentle irrigation improves visibility.

Typical Clinical Features
Classic triad: severe pain + empty socket + delayed onset 2–5 days post-extraction. Highly suggestive of alveolar osteitis.

Red Flags ⚠️
Reconsider diagnosis if: facial swelling, fever, trismus, pus discharge, progressive swelling, difficulty swallowing, failure to improve after local management, severe pain beyond 2 weeks. Suggests alternative diagnosis or secondary infection.

Investigations
Most require no investigations.
Radiographs: Consider PA or OPG if suspect retained root, tooth fragment, fractured bone, foreign material, alternative pathology. Routine imaging unnecessary in straightforward cases.

Management
Step 1 – Gentle Irrigation: Warm saline to remove food debris. Avoid vigorous curettage — may delay healing.
Step 2 – Pain Relief: Appropriate analgesia per patient needs and PMH. Advise regular analgesia.
Step 3 – Socket Dressing: Depending on local practice, obtundant dressing may be placed for temporary pain relief. Reduces exposed bone sensitivity. May need review/replacement. Clinicians should know products used locally.
Step 4 – Patient Advice: Explain: painful but self-limiting, healing 7–14 days, pain should gradually improve, gentle rinsing after 24h, smoking delays healing. Reassurance is therapeutic.

Antibiotics
Routine antibiotics NOT indicated. Consider only if: cellulitis, spreading infection, systemic illness, immunocompromise with concern for secondary infection. Prescribing for uncomplicated dry socket exposes patients to adverse effects without benefit.

Follow-Up
Review if: pain remains severe, repeat dressing needed, symptoms worsen, diagnosis uncertain. Most improve substantially within days.

Admission
Almost never required. Consider only if: significant spreading infection develops, severe medical comorbidity complicates management, alternative pathology requires inpatient care.

DCT Checklist: Before You Phone Your Registrar
□ Which tooth extracted?
□ Date of extraction?
□ Timing of pain onset?
□ Presence/absence of swelling?
□ Socket appearance?
□ Exposed bone?
□ Pus?
□ Temperature and obs?
□ Radiographs taken?
□ Another diagnosis suspected?

sections.heading: Key Takeaways
items: Dry socket presents 2–5 days post-extraction with severe pain, minimal swelling, empty socket

title: Post-Extraction Haemorrhage
quote: Most post-extraction bleeding can be controlled with simple measures. The skill is recognising when simple measures are no longer enough.

items:
Why This Matters
Post-extraction haemorrhage is one of the commonest emergency OMFS presentations. Most patients arrive anxious, frightened and convinced they are "bleeding to death", when in reality they have persistent oozing mixed with saliva. However, a small number have significant haemorrhage requiring prompt intervention, particularly those on anticoagulants, with bleeding disorders, or after difficult surgical extractions. Your role: assess patient not just socket, determine if true haemorrhage or blood-stained saliva, identify cause, achieve haemostasis, recognise when senior help required. Calm, systematic approach manages vast majority.

sections.heading: Golden Rule
items: Pressure stops most bleeding. Panic stops nothing. Before reaching for haemostatic agents or calling theatre, ensure effective local pressure has been applied correctly.

sections.heading: Core Content
items:
Understanding Post-Extraction Haemorrhage
Primary: During procedure. Managed immediately.
Reactionary: Within 24h. Most common presentation to OMFS. Due to loss of vasoconstrictor, rising BP, inadequate clot, clot dislodgement.
Secondary: Several days later. Usually infection, clot breakdown, delayed healing. Much less common.

Initial Assessment – ABCDE
Airway: Ensure clear. Large volumes swallowed → nausea/vomiting. Profuse bleeding: sit upright, spit into bowl not swallow.
Breathing: RR, SpO2, associated chest injuries.
Circulation: Priority. Document pulse, BP, CRT, skin colour. Ask: "Have you felt dizzy or faint?" "How many gauzes/towels soaked?" "Have you fainted?" Persistent tachycardia/hypotension → urgent senior review.
Disability: GCS, symptoms of hypovolaemia.
Exposure: Estimate blood loss, ongoing bleeding, bruising elsewhere.

History
Presenting Complaint: Is bleeding continuous? Did it stop and restart? Gradually worsened?
Dental History: Which tooth removed? Simple or surgical? Bone removed? Sutures placed? Bleeding difficult during extraction?
Medical History: Anticoagulants (DOACs/warfarin), antiplatelets, liver disease, renal disease, bleeding disorders, previous prolonged bleeding, chemo, alcohol excess. Never assume "not on blood thinners" excludes bleeding disorder.
Medication History: Name, dose, time of last dose of anticoagulant. INR if warfarin. Also aspirin, clopidogrel, DAPT, herbal supplements increasing bleeding risk.

Examination
General: Well, pale, anxious, haemodynamically unstable? Document obs before focusing on socket.
Intraoral: Good lighting + suction essential. First remove excess clot gently to identify source. Assess: active arterial bleeding, venous oozing, socket clot, torn gingiva, lacerations, loose sutures, retained roots, sharp bone. Do not assume extraction socket is only source.

Is It Really Bleeding?
Many describe: "My mouth is full of blood." Often saliva lightly stained with blood. Ask patient to rinse gently then observe socket directly. Simple step often prevents unnecessary intervention.

Investigations
Most require no investigations.
Bloods: If significant blood loss, medical comorbidity, admission likely. FBC, U&E, G&S if major bleeding, coagulation screen where clinically indicated.
INR: Only relevant for warfarin. Recent therapeutic INR does not exclude local causes but guides management.

Stepwise Management
Step 1 – Direct Pressure: Single most important intervention. Place folded damp gauze directly over socket. Patient bites firmly 20–30 minutes without checking. Every time clot disturbed, bleeding may restart.
Step 2 – Local Anaesthetic: If further intervention needed: LA with vasoconstrictor unless contraindicated. Benefits: pain relief, improved access, vasoconstriction, better cooperation.
Step 3 – Identify Bleeding Source: Carefully inspect: socket bleeding, soft tissue tears, bone bleeding, arterial bleeders, retained granulation tissue. Treat cause not just cover socket.
Step 4 – Local Haemostatic Measures: Depending on availability/local practice: resuture socket, absorbable haemostatic materials (oxidised regenerated cellulose, collagen, gelatin-based), firm socket packing, additional pressure. Choice depends on situation and protocols.
Step 5 – Reassess: Observe several minutes. If haemostasis achieved: instructions, follow-up if required. If bleeding persists: escalate to registrar.

Tranexamic Acid
TXA mouthwash may be used in selected patients per local protocols, particularly those at increased bleeding risk. Follow local guidelines.

Patients Taking Anticoagulants
Most extractions safely performed without stopping anticoagulants when protocols followed. When reviewing bleeding patient: Do NOT advise stopping anticoagulants without senior discussion. Instead: achieve local haemostasis, assess haemodynamic status, discuss persistent bleeding with reg. More on anticoagulants in separate teaching session.

When Should You Admit?
Consider if: bleeding cannot be controlled, repeated intervention required, significant blood loss, haemodynamically unstable, significant comorbidity, social circumstances unsafe, GA may be required for haemostasis.

Discharge Advice
Before discharge ensure patient understands: bite firmly on gauze if bleeding recurs, avoid vigorous rinsing first 24h after treatment, avoid smoking, avoid strenuous exercise remainder of day, sleep head elevated if possible, return immediately if bleeding heavy/continuous. Provide written instructions.

Red Flags ⚠️
Admit/urgent senior review: uncontrolled bleeding despite pressure + local measures, tachycardia/hypotension, >5 soaked gauzes, dizziness/syncope, known bleeding disorder, INR >4 on warfarin with active bleed, liver disease, posterior bleed not visualised.

title: Dentoalveolar Trauma
quote: Time is tissue. The earlier dentoalveolar injuries are recognised and managed appropriately, the better the long-term outcome for both teeth and supporting structures.

items:
Why This Matters
Dentoalveolar injuries account for a significant proportion of emergency OMFS referrals, particularly in children, adolescents and young adults. They commonly result from falls, sporting injuries, assaults, road traffic collisions and recreational accidents. Unlike many other OMFS emergencies, the success of treatment is often determined by how quickly and how accurately the injury is managed. Delayed diagnosis, inappropriate splinting or failure to reposition displaced teeth can result in pulpal necrosis, ankylosis, root resorption and ultimately tooth loss. Your role: exclude life-threatening injuries, perform systematic dental/facial assessment, identify injury type, reposition and stabilise teeth where indicated, arrange follow-up. Remember: the patient is more important than the tooth.

sections.heading: Golden Rule
items: Treat the patient before treating the tooth. A fractured incisor should never distract you from a cervical spine injury or significant facial trauma.

sections.heading: Core Content
items:
BEFORE YOU PHONE YOUR REGISTRAR
Know: □ Mechanism of injury, □ LOC?, □ C-spine concern?, □ Which teeth involved?, □ Are any teeth missing?, □ Aspiration/ingestion excluded?, □ Are teeth displaced?, □ Is there alveolar fracture?, □ Radiographs obtained?, □ Does patient require splinting?

Initial Trauma Assessment – ATLS Principles
Airway: Patency, facial bleeding, loose teeth, avulsed teeth, foreign bodies. Remove loose fragments only if airway risk.
Breathing: RR, SpO2, chest injuries.
Circulation: BP, pulse, active bleeding. Control facial haemorrhage with direct pressure.
Disability: GCS, pupils, neuro status. Ask: LOC, vomiting, amnesia.
Exposure: Facial lacerations, bruising, swelling, other injuries. Never assume dental trauma occurs in isolation.

History
Mechanism: Fall, assault, sport, bicycle, RTC — predicts injury pattern.
Timing: Exactly when did injury occur? Critical for avulsed teeth.
LOC: Black out, vomiting, confusion? Head injury may take precedence.
Missing Teeth: "Do you know where every tooth is?" If not, consider aspiration, ingestion, intrusion. Missing tooth never simply assumed lost at scene.
Medical History: Anticoagulants, bleeding disorders, tetanus status for contaminated injuries.

Examination
Extraoral: Facial asymmetry, swelling, lacerations, bruising. Palpate: orbital rims, zygomas, nasal bones, mandible. Assess mandibular movements.
Cranial Nerves: Document infraorbital nerve, mental nerve, facial nerve where indicated.
Intraoral: Missing teeth, tooth mobility, displacement, fractures, gingival lacerations, occlusion, bite changes. Always compare with opposite side.

sections.heading: Classification of Dental Injuries
items:
Alveolar Fractures
Assess for: segment mobility, occlusal changes, gingival lacerations. Teeth often move as one unit. Treatment: repositioning, flexible splinting, soft diet, OMFS follow-up.

sections.heading: Inability to achieve normal occlusion after repositioning
items:
Investigations
Radiographs: Periapical, OPG, occlusal views depending on injury.
CT Imaging: If facial fractures suspected, multiple injuries, high-energy trauma, significant alveolar fractures.
CXR: If tooth missing and aspiration cannot be excluded.

Soft Tissue Injuries
Always inspect lips carefully. Lacerations frequently contain tooth fragments/enamel/foreign material. Failure to remove embedded fragments causes delayed complications. Radiograph lip if fragment unaccounted for.

Splinting Principles
Current evidence supports flexible splinting for most dentoalveolar injuries. Rigid splints avoided unless specifically indicated, e.g. certain alveolar fractures. Duration depends on injury type — follow current international guidance (IADT).

Antibiotics
Routine antibiotics NOT indicated for every dental injury. Consider in: avulsed teeth, contaminated wounds, associated soft tissue injuries. Follow local protocols and current trauma guidelines.

Tetanus
Consider prophylaxis for: contaminated injuries, soil contamination, animal-related injuries. Follow national guidance.

Admission Criteria
Uncommon but consider if: associated facial fractures, significant soft tissue injuries, airway concerns, multiple injuries, GA required, safeguarding concerns, significant head injury.

Discharge Advice
Advise: soft diet 1–2 weeks, excellent OH, chlorhexidine mouthwash if appropriate, avoid contact sports, attend all follow-up, return if increasing mobility/swelling/pain.
