title: Avulsed Permanent Teeth
quote: Every minute a permanent tooth remains dry reduces the chance of successful replantation. Time is the most important treatment.

items:
Why This Matters
Avulsion is the complete displacement of a tooth from its socket and is one of the few true dental emergencies. No other dentoalveolar injury is so critically dependent on time. Prognosis depends largely on survival of periodontal ligament (PDL) cells attached to the root surface. These cells begin to lose viability as soon as the tooth dries out. Immediate replantation offers the greatest chance of long-term survival, while prolonged dry storage significantly increases risks of inflammatory root resorption and ankylosis. Your priorities: confirm this is a permanent tooth, minimise extra-oral dry time, replant ASAP where appropriate, stabilise, arrange follow-up. The clock starts the moment the tooth leaves the socket—not when the patient arrives.

sections.heading: Golden Rule
items: Never scrub the root. Protect the periodontal ligament. The root surface contains viable PDL cells essential for healing.

sections.heading: Core Content
items:
BEFORE YOU PHONE YOUR REGISTRAR
Know: □ Permanent or primary tooth?, □ When did injury occur?, □ How long out of mouth?, □ Stored correctly?, □ Replanted already?, □ Socket intact?, □ Associated alveolar fracture?, □ Aspiration excluded?, □ Splinting required?, □ Tetanus prophylaxis required?

The First Question: Is It a Permanent Tooth?
This is the most important question.
Permanent Tooth: Usually replant if appropriate.
Primary Tooth: Never replant. Risks damage to developing permanent successor. This is one of the highest-yield facts in exams and on-call.

The Biology of Avulsion
Long-term prognosis depends on: PDL cell survival, root surface integrity, extra-oral dry time, storage medium, stage of root development. Pulpal survival is secondary to preservation of PDL.

Time Matters
Prognosis worsens as extra-oral dry time increases.
<15 minutes: Excellent prognosis. Immediate replantation ideal.
<60 minutes: Good chance of periodontal healing if stored appropriately.
>60 minutes dry: PDL survival poor. Replantation still usually indicated for permanent teeth, but counsel re high risk of ankylosis/replacement resorption. Delayed replantation may still preserve alveolar bone and provide functional/aesthetic benefits, particularly in younger patients.

sections.heading: Patient’s saliva – buccal sulcus if conscious/cooperative
items:
Normal saline
Avoid plain water — damages PDL cells due to low osmolarity.

Initial Assessment – ABCDE
Airway: Ensure no fragments threaten airway. If tooth missing, always consider aspiration, ingestion, intrusion.
Breathing: Assess for thoracic injury if significant trauma.
Circulation: Control facial bleeding. Assess other injuries.
Disability: GCS, head injury symptoms, LOC.
Exposure: Facial lacerations, alveolar fractures, other dental injuries.

History
Ask: Exact time of injury, mechanism, where tooth kept, was it cleaned, any replantation attempt, LOC, vomiting, other facial injuries.
PMH: Immunocompromise, bleeding disorders, tetanus status.

Examination
Extraoral: Facial injuries, lip lacerations, swelling, bruising. Always palpate for facial fractures.
Intraoral: Empty socket, socket integrity, alveolar fractures, gingival lacerations, occlusion, other damaged teeth. Inspect avulsed tooth. Do not scrape root. Handle by crown only.

Immediate Management
Step 1: Confirm tooth is permanent.
Step 2: Rinse visible debris gently with sterile saline if required. Do NOT scrub, curette, or remove attached PDL tissue.
Step 3: LA if required. Inspect socket. Remove only obvious clot preventing replantation. Do NOT aggressively curette socket.
Step 4: Replant tooth gently with firm digital pressure. Ensure correct orientation. Tooth should seat fully.
Step 5: Confirm position clinically. Assess occlusion.
Step 6: Apply passive flexible splint. Current IADT guidance: ∼2 weeks for uncomplicated avulsion. Longer if associated alveolar fracture.
Step 7: Arrange follow-up with appropriate dental trauma service.

Antibiotics
Systemic antibiotics generally recommended following replantation of avulsed permanent tooth, particularly where contamination occurred. Choice follows local protocols and current IADT guidelines, considering age, PMH, allergies, pregnancy.

Tetanus
Assess tetanus status. Contaminated injuries may require vaccination/booster per national guidance.

Radiographs
Usually: periapical, occlusal, OPG if multiple injuries. Assess: tooth position, root fracture, alveolar fracture, intrusion of adjacent teeth.

Red Flags ⚠️
Do NOT replant if: primary tooth, patient medically unfit, extensive alveolar fracture preventing stability, tooth grossly contaminated and cannot be cleaned without damaging PDL, significant medical contraindication. Discuss with senior.
Urgent senior review if: cannot achieve replantation, associated facial fractures, airway concern, aspiration suspected, significant head injury.

Complications
Discuss possibility of: pulp necrosis, inflammatory root resorption, replacement resorption, ankylosis, tooth loss. May develop months/years later despite optimal treatment.

Follow-Up
Long-term review required. Typical follow-up: clinical exam, pulp sensibility testing, radiographs at 2 weeks, 4 weeks, 3 months, 6 months, 1 year, then yearly. May continue several years.

Admission
Rarely required unless: associated facial fractures, significant head injury, GA required, multiple injuries, safeguarding concerns.

sections.heading: Handle tooth by crown only — never touch/scrub root surface
items: If immediate replantation impossible, store in milk, HBSS, saliva or saline — never in water
Flexible splinting + long-term follow-up essential for all replanted permanent teeth

Registrar Handover Prompt

Structure: “8yo, UL1 avulsed 25min ago playing football. Stored in milk. Replanted on arrival, now in position, flexible splint applied. No head injury. OPG shows no root # or alveolar #. Tetanus up to date, given co-amoxiclav per local protocol. Plan dental trauma clinic 2/52.”

sections.heading:
DCT Survival Box 🚨
The Three Rules of Avulsion
items: Permanent teeth are usually replanted.
Primary teeth are never replanted.

Never hold the tooth by the root.
If you remember these three rules, you will avoid the commonest mistakes.

title: Mandibular Fractures
quote: Treat the patient first, the fracture second. Airway, occlusion and associated injuries always take priority over the radiograph.

items:
Why This Matters
Mandibular fractures are among the commonest facial fractures managed by OMFS. Frequently encountered following assaults, falls, sporting injuries and RTCs. Most are not immediately life-threatening but may be associated with airway compromise, significant haemorrhage, cervical spine injury, intracranial injury, or other facial fractures. Your role is not simply to identify a fracture on imaging — it is to assess the entire patient, recognise associated injuries and communicate findings effectively to seniors. A patient with a normal CT but an unrecognised airway problem is far more dangerous than a patient with a mandibular fracture waiting for surgery.

sections.heading: Golden Rule
items: The most important examination finding in a mandibular fracture is the patient's occlusion. If the bite is normal, significant displacement is less likely. If the bite has changed, assume a fracture until proven otherwise.

sections.heading: Core Content
items:
BEFORE YOU PHONE YOUR REGISTRAR
Know: □ Mechanism of injury, □ LOC?, □ C-spine concerns?, □ Airway normal?, □ Patient's occlusion?, □ Trismus?, □ Numbness of lower lip/chin?, □ Open fracture?, □ Imaging shows?, □ Other facial fractures?

Relevant Anatomy
The mandible forms a ring-like structure. A force strong enough to fracture the mandible often produces a second fracture elsewhere. Always actively search for additional fractures. Common sites: condyle, angle, body, parasymphysis, symphysis, ramus, coronoid process.

Mechanisms of Injury
Assault: Most common cause in many OMFS units. Frequently causes angle fractures and parasymphysis fractures.
Falls: More common in children/elderly. Frequently associated with condylar injuries.
Sporting Injuries: Often isolated fractures.
RTC: High-energy. Often associated with multiple fractures, head injury, C-spine injury.

Initial Assessment – ABCDE
Airway: Patency, facial swelling, oral bleeding, loose teeth, foreign bodies. Look for posterior displacement of fractured segments, bilateral parasymphyseal fractures causing tongue displacement, expanding floor of mouth haematoma. Airway compromise uncommon but potentially life-threatening.
Breathing: RR, SpO2, chest injuries.
Circulation: Pulse, BP, active bleeding. Most mandibular fractures bleed modestly, but significant oral bleeding can occur.
Disability: GCS, pupils, head injury symptoms. Ask: LOC, vomiting, amnesia.
Exposure: Other injuries, facial lacerations, limb injuries, neck injuries.

History
Mechanism: How did injury occur? Punch to jaw ≠ bicycle accident.
Timing: When did injury happen?
Symptoms: Pain, malocclusion, trismus, numbness, difficulty chewing, difficulty speaking. Patient's description of altered occlusion is highly reliable.

Examination
General Inspection: Facial asymmetry, swelling, bruising, lacerations. Look from front and above.
Occlusion: Most important part. Ask: "Do your teeth meet together normally?" Assess directly. Look for premature contact, open bite, midline shift, crossbite, new malocclusion. Document carefully.
Palpation: Symphysis, parasymphysis, body, angle, ramus, condyles. Assess tenderness, step deformity, crepitus, mobility.
Mouth Opening: Measure and document. Reduced opening may indicate pain, muscle spasm, condylar injury, coronoid injury.
Intraoral: Gingival tears, haematoma, step deformity, tooth fractures, mobile segments. Sublingual haematoma = classic sign of mandibular fracture.
Inferior Alveolar Nerve: Assess lower lip/chin sensation. Document carefully. Mental nerve paraesthesia common with body/angle fractures.

sections.heading: Common Fracture Patterns
items:
Open vs Closed Fractures
Mandibular fracture considered open if it communicates with: oral cavity, skin laceration, PDL space of tooth-bearing segment. Most dentate mandibular fractures are effectively open fractures. Implications for antibiotics and definitive management.

Red Flags 🚩
Urgent senior review if: airway compromise, bilateral mandibular fractures, significant displacement, open fracture with contamination, associated facial fractures, neurological deficit, polytrauma, uncontrolled haemorrhage.

Investigations
OPG: Useful for initial assessment, fracture location, dentition assessment. Limitations: less useful for condyles, may underestimate complex injuries.
CT Facial Bones: Investigation of choice. Provides fracture location, degree of displacement, additional facial fractures, surgical planning information. Now standard in most trauma centres.

Initial Management
Analgesia: Provide appropriate pain relief early.
Soft Diet: Advise soft diet, avoid chewing hard foods.
Oral Hygiene: Recommend good OH, antiseptic mouth rinses where appropriate.
Antibiotics: Follow local protocols. Many units prescribe for open mandibular fractures, particularly with oral cavity communication. Practice varies.

Definitive Management
Depends on: fracture location, degree of displacement, occlusion, dentition, patient factors.
Conservative: Selected minimally displaced fractures with stable occlusion.
Closed Reduction: Arch bars, IMF.
ORIF: Titanium plates/screws. Indications: displacement, malocclusion, unstable fractures, multiple fractures.

Admission Criteria
Consider if: airway concerns, polytrauma, significant pain, inability to maintain oral intake, requirement for surgery, social concerns. Many admitted pending operative treatment.

Discharge Criteria
Selected patients discharged if: airway stable, pain controlled, oral intake adequate, clear follow-up arranged, definitive treatment planning occurred. Provide clear advice re worsening pain, swelling or occlusion changes.

items: Assess patient using trauma principles before focusing on fracture — ABCDE first

sections.heading: Occlusion is the most important clinical finding in mandibular trauma
items: Always look for a second mandibular fracture — ring structure means forces often cause two

sections.heading: CT is imaging of choice, but management guided by patient not just scan
items:
Registrar Handover Prompt
Structure: Mechanism, airway status, LOC, occlusion, mouth opening, IAN status, open/closed, CT findings, associated injuries, plan. If you can’t answer “What is the patient’s occlusion like?” you have not completed the examination. Consultants agree: mandibular fracture assessment is incomplete without occlusion documented.

title: Midface Fractures
quote: The eye, the occlusion and the airway matter more than the fracture pattern. Always assess function before classification.

items:
Why This Matters
Midface fractures range from isolated nasal fractures to complex panfacial injuries involving maxilla, zygoma, orbit and skull base. For new DCTs, it’s easy to become distracted by CT classifications. The first priorities are simpler: Is the airway safe? Can the patient see normally? Is there an ocular emergency? Is the occlusion altered? Is there a CSF leak? Only after these are answered should you describe fracture patterns. You are treating an injured patient—not a CT scan.

sections.heading: Golden Rule
items: Every patient with a midface fracture deserves an eye examination. Failure to examine and document vision is one of the commonest and most serious errors in facial trauma.

sections.heading: Core Content
items:
BEFORE YOU PHONE YOUR REGISTRAR
Know: □ Airway stable?, □ Visual acuity each eye?, □ Pupils equal/reactive?, □ Diplopia?, □ Eye movements full?, □ Reduced V2 sensation?, □ Occlusion normal?, □ CSF leak?, □ Which bones fractured?, □ Urgent ophthalmology needed?

Initial Assessment – ATLS Principles
Airway: Blood, loose teeth, facial swelling, posterior displacement of fractures, vomiting. High-energy facial injuries may rapidly compromise airway.
Breathing: RR, SpO2, associated chest injuries.
Circulation: Pulse, BP, external bleeding. Control facial bleeding with direct pressure.
Disability: GCS, pupils, head injury symptoms. Ask: LOC, vomiting, amnesia.
Exposure: Facial asymmetry, bruising, lacerations, other traumatic injuries.

History
Mechanism: Punch, fall, RTC, sport. Mechanism predicts pattern.
Time of injury.
Visual symptoms: Loss of vision, double vision, blurred vision, floaters.
Facial numbness: Cheek, upper lip, side of nose.
Difficulty biting: Altered occlusion.
Epistaxis: Unilateral/bilateral, persistent.
Previous facial fractures.
PMH: Anticoagulants, bleeding disorders, relevant ophthalmic history — glaucoma, previous surgery, monocular vision.

The Eye Examination
This is mandatory. Document every component. Do it before swelling makes assessment impossible.

Red Flags 🚩
Urgent senior + ophthalmology review if: reduced visual acuity, RAPD, suspected globe rupture, retrobulbar haemorrhage, progressive proptosis, severe restriction of eye movements, entrapment especially in children, hyphaema. These are true emergencies.

Retrobulbar Haemorrhage
Orbital compartment syndrome. Signs: severe pain, proptosis, tense orbit, reduced VA, RAPD, ophthalmoplegia. Requires emergency lateral canthotomy/cantholysis. Time critical — minutes to irreversible visual loss.

Facial Examination
Palpation: Frontal bone, supraorbital rims, infraorbital rims, zygomatic arches, nasal bones, maxilla. Look for step deformities, tenderness, crepitus, mobility.
Occlusion: Ask patient to bite together. Assess premature contacts, open bite, crossbite, mobility of maxilla. Malocclusion suggests significant skeletal injury. Mobile maxilla is never normal.
V2 Sensation: Lower eyelid, cheek, side of nose, upper lip. Reduced sensation common in ZMC and orbital floor fractures.

sections.heading: Common Midface Fractures
items:
Septal Haematoma
Blood collection between septal cartilage and mucoperichondrium. Exam: bilateral boggy swelling of septum, bluish discolouration. Must drain urgently — untreated causes septal necrosis and saddle-nose deformity. Use nasal speculum + headlight.

CSF Rhinorrhoea
Clear fluid from nose. Ask: salty taste, worse leaning forward. Test: halo sign, glucose positive, beta-2 transferrin. Indicates skull base fracture. Needs neurosurgery discussion.

Investigations
CT Facial Bones: Imaging of choice. Shows fracture pattern, displacement, orbital involvement, associated facial fractures. Review yourself before calling reg.
Additional Imaging: CT Head, CT C-spine, CT Angiography if vascular injury suspected.

sections.heading: OH advice — gentle, chlorhexidine if tolerated
items: Antibiotics: Follow local protocols for open fractures. Not routine for all.
Advise: Do NOT blow nose if orbital fracture suspected — risk of orbital emphysema and visual compromise. Avoid straining, heavy lifting.

When Should You Admit?
Airway compromise, significant ocular injury, retrobulbar haemorrhage, CSF leak, multiple facial fractures, severe pain requiring inpatient management, associated head injury, requirement for urgent surgery.

Discharge Criteria
Vision normal, no ocular emergency, pain controlled, oral intake adequate, follow-up arranged, understand return precautions. Safety-net: immediate return if worsening vision, increasing pain, new diplopia, persistent clear nasal discharge, increasing swelling, difficulty breathing.

items: Every midface fracture patient needs documented eye exam — VA, pupils, EOM, diplopia

sections.heading: Visual acuity recorded before anything else in ophthalmic assessment
items: Assess occlusion in every facial trauma patient — malocclusion = significant injury
Never miss septal haematoma or retrobulbar haemorrhage — both cause permanent damage if delayed
Treat function first — vision, airway, occlusion matter more than memorising classifications

Registrar Handover Prompt
Lead with function: “30M, assault. No airway concern. VA 6/6 R, 6/9 L. No RAPD. Restricted upgaze L with diplopia. V2 paraesthesia L. Occlusion stable. CT: L orbital floor + ZMC #. Needs ophthalmology review for entrapment. For admission and probable theatre.”
Avoid: “He’s got a Le Fort II.” Start with what worries you: “Airway safe. Worried about vision — VA reduced and RAPD present.”

sections.heading: Check the occlusion
items:
Look for a septal haematoma
Do these four consistently and you avoid the commonest and most serious mistakes.

title: Orbital Injuries and Retrobulbar Haemorrhage
quote: The patient who loses vision from an untreated retrobulbar haemorrhage has suffered a preventable complication. Recognise it early, act decisively and call for help immediately.

items:
Why This Matters
Orbital injuries are common following facial trauma, but retrobulbar haemorrhage (RBH) is rare. Despite its rarity, every OMFS DCT must recognise it because it is one of the few true sight-threatening emergencies in maxillofacial surgery. Bleeding behind the globe rapidly increases intraorbital pressure, producing orbital compartment syndrome. As pressure rises, optic nerve and retinal perfusion fall. If not relieved promptly, irreversible visual loss may occur within hours. The diagnosis is clinical. Do not wait for a CT scan if orbital compartment syndrome is strongly suspected. Your priorities: recognise the condition, assess vision immediately, escalate to reg + ophthalmology without delay, prepare for emergency lateral canthotomy + inferior cantholysis if indicated. Never allow imaging to delay sight-saving treatment.

sections.heading: Golden Rule
items: Vision first. CT later. If orbital compartment syndrome is suspected clinically, decompression should not be delayed while awaiting imaging.

sections.heading: Core Content
items:
BEFORE YOU PHONE YOUR REGISTRAR
Know: □ Visual acuity each eye?, □ Pupils equal?, □ RAPD present?, □ Eye proptosed?, □ Eye movements restricted?, □ Diplopia?, □ Globe tense on gentle palpation through closed lid?, □ Increasing pain?, □ When did injury occur?, □ Has ophthalmology been informed?

What Is a Retrobulbar Haemorrhage?
Bleeding into orbital space behind the globe. Orbit is a confined bony compartment — even small volume of blood causes marked rise in intraorbital pressure → compression of optic nerve, compression of retinal circulation, orbital compartment syndrome, permanent blindness.

Causes
Facial trauma, orbital fractures, orbital surgery, peribulbar/retrobulbar anaesthetic injections, endoscopic sinus surgery, anticoagulation, spontaneous bleeding (rare).

Initial Assessment – ABCDE
Orbital injuries frequently occur with multiple injuries. Always complete trauma assessment first.
Airway: Facial swelling, bleeding, associated fractures.
Breathing: Respiratory status.
Circulation: Control major bleeding, document obs.
Disability: GCS, head injury symptoms.
Exposure: Inspect entire face. Orbital injuries frequently occur alongside ZMC, Le Fort, nasal fractures.

History
Ask: exact mechanism, time of onset of visual symptoms, has vision deteriorated, double vision, eye pain, pain on eye movement, previous eye disease, contact lens use, anticoagulants. Sudden deterioration after initially normal vision is particularly concerning.

The Eye Examination – <2 Minutes
Visual Acuity: Most important finding. Test each eye separately. Use Snellen chart, reading text, counting fingers, hand movements, perception of light. Never document "Vision appears normal".
Pupils: Equality, direct/consensual responses, RAPD. An RAPD strongly suggests optic nerve dysfunction.
Eye Movements: All directions. Restricted upward gaze may suggest muscle entrapment, orbital swelling, or compartment syndrome.
Diplopia: Ask: "Do you see one image or two?" Determine: constant?, direction of gaze?
Visual Fields: Confrontation testing if possible.
Globe Position: Proptosis, enophthalmos, vertical dystopia. Rapidly progressive proptosis highly concerning.
Eyelids: Tense swollen eyelids, ecchymosis, lacerations. Rock-hard swollen eyelid should immediately raise suspicion of orbital compartment syndrome.
IOP: If available and no suspicion of globe rupture, IOP measurement supports diagnosis. Do NOT delay treatment to obtain this.

sections.heading: Raised IOP
items:
Reduced visual fields
One abnormality may warrant urgent senior review.

sections.heading: Pupil Abnormality — RAPD
items:
Pressure — tense orbit/raised IOP
If present after facial trauma, escalate immediately.

Investigations
CT Facial Bones: Demonstrates orbital fractures, RBH, globe displacement, muscle entrapment. However: normal CT performed later does not reverse permanent visual loss. If diagnosis clinically obvious, treatment takes priority over imaging.

Emergency Management
Step 1: Call immediately — your registrar, ophthalmology, anaesthetic support if required.
Step 2: Assess and document: vision, pupils, RAPD, eye movements. Repeat frequently.
Step 3: Elevate head to ∼30°. Avoid unnecessary pressure on eye.
Step 4: If orbital compartment syndrome strongly suspected and senior help not immediately available: prepare for emergency lateral canthotomy + inferior cantholysis. This is a sight-saving procedure. Every OMFS trainee must understand why, when, and anatomy. Even if not yet performing independently, recognise when it cannot wait.

Lateral Canthotomy and Inferior Cantholysis
Indications: Suspected orbital compartment syndrome with visual deterioration, RAPD, proptosis, tense orbit, raised orbital pressure.
Principle: Releases lateral canthal tendon, allowing globe to move forward, reducing orbital pressure. Does not treat haemorrhage. Buys time to preserve optic nerve perfusion.
Note: This is covered in practical skills sessions. Do not attempt without senior guidance unless life/limb/sight threat and no senior immediately available.

Medical Therapy
Adjuncts may be considered following senior discussion per local protocols: mannitol, acetazolamide, high-dose steroids. These do NOT replace surgical decompression where orbital compartment syndrome is present.

Globe Rupture
Always consider. Features: irregular pupil, low IOP, hyphaema, uveal prolapse, obvious penetrating injury, positive Seidel test. If suspected: do NOT apply pressure, shield the eye, urgent ophthalmology review.

Admission
Most patients with suspected RBH require admission for monitoring and ophthalmology input.

sections.heading: The diagnosis is clinical — do not wait for imaging
items: CT should never delay decompression when orbital compartment syndrome is suspected

sections.heading: Key Takeaways
items: Retrobulbar haemorrhage causing orbital compartment syndrome is a true sight-threatening emergency
Visual acuity and pupil exam should be performed immediately and documented clearly — these are your baselines
An RAPD, deteriorating vision and tense proptosed eye trigger immediate senior escalation
Do not delay treatment while waiting for CT if orbital compartment syndrome strongly suspected
Lateral canthotomy + inferior cantholysis are sight-saving — every OMFS trainee must understand indications

Registrar Handover Prompt
Lead with vision: “Assault 1 hour ago. RE visual acuity counting fingers only, was 6/6 earlier. RAPD present. Proptosed, tense orbit, pain on movement. Suspected orbital compartment syndrome. Ophthalmology called. Requesting immediate review for lateral canthotomy.” Fracture pattern is secondary to functional deficit.

Clinical Pearl – The Consultant's Question
If asked: "What finding would make you most worried?"
The answer is not: "A fractured orbit."
It is: "A patient with deteriorating vision, RAPD, progressive proptosis and a tense orbit. Those findings indicate orbital compartment syndrome until proven otherwise and require immediate decompression." The fracture can wait. The optic nerve cannot.

title: Zygomaticomaxillary Complex (ZMC) Fractures
quote: A flattened cheek, infraorbital numbness and diplopia should immediately make you think of a zygomaticomaxillary complex fracture. Always assess function before deciding on treatment.

items:
Why This Matters
The zygomaticomaxillary complex, often called the cheekbone, is one of the most frequently fractured regions of the facial skeleton. Common after assaults, falls, sporting injuries and RTCs. Although many ZMC fractures appear dramatic due to swelling, your job is not simply to identify the fracture on CT. The real priorities are determining whether the injury has affected vision, eye movements, globe position, infraorbital nerve function, mouth opening, and facial symmetry. Many minimally displaced fractures are managed conservatively. Displaced fractures causing functional or cosmetic deformity usually require surgery.

sections.heading: Golden Rule
items: Always examine the eye before examining the CT scan. A perfectly reduced fracture is of little value if an ocular injury has been missed.

sections.heading: Core Content
items:
BEFORE YOU PHONE YOUR REGISTRAR
Know: □ Mechanism of injury, □ Visual acuity, □ Diplopia?, □ Eye movements?, □ Globe position normal?, □ Infraorbital nerve sensation?, □ Mouth opening?, □ Palpable step deformity?, □ Fracture displaced on CT?, □ Is ophthalmology required?

Anatomy You Need to Understand
The zygoma forms the prominence of the cheek and contributes to: lateral orbital wall, orbital floor, zygomatic arch, anterior maxillary buttress. A ZMC fracture usually involves separation at four articulations: frontozygomatic suture, zygomaticomaxillary buttress, zygomaticotemporal articulation (arch), orbital floor/lateral orbital wall. You don’t need to identify all four clinically, but understanding this explains why displacement affects both facial contour and orbital anatomy.

Initial Assessment – ATLS Principles
Always ABCDE before focusing on the face. Patients with sufficient force to fracture the zygoma may also have: head injury, C-spine injury, mandibular fractures, orbital injuries, thoracic trauma.

History
Mechanism: Assault, sport, fall, RTC? Direct blows to cheek typical.
Symptoms: Cheek pain, facial swelling, flattening of cheek, double vision, numb upper lip/cheek, difficulty opening mouth, pain on chewing, cosmetic asymmetry.
Visual Symptoms: Always ask: Is vision blurred? Double vision? Is one eye sitting differently? Any flashes or floaters? Visual symptoms require careful assessment.

Examination
Inspection: Look from front and above. Assess: facial asymmetry, loss of malar prominence, periorbital bruising, subconjunctival haemorrhage (especially without visible posterior limit), eyelid swelling, lacerations. Flattened cheek may become more obvious as swelling settles.

The Eye Examination — Mandatory in every patient. Document every component.
Visual Acuity: Test each eye separately. Document formally. Never omit. If no chart: reading print, counting fingers, hand movements, or perception of light.
Pupils: Size, equality, direct/consensual responses, RAPD. RAPD = important sign of optic nerve injury.
Eye Movements: Assess all directions. Restricted upward gaze may indicate orbital floor involvement or muscle entrapment. Significant displacement.
Diplopia: Ask specifically: “Do you see double?” Determine if constant, only on upward gaze, or in primary gaze. Diplopia in primary gaze has greater functional significance.
Visual Fields: Confrontation testing if possible.
Globe Position: Assess enophthalmos, proptosis, vertical dystopia. Compare both eyes from above.

Red Flags 🚩
Urgent senior review + ophthalmology if: reduced visual acuity, RAPD, suspected globe rupture, retrobulbar haemorrhage, progressive proptosis, severe restriction of eye movements, entrapment particularly in children, hyphaema. These are true emergencies.

Facial Examination
Palpation: Infraorbital rim, zygomatic arch, frontozygomatic region, zygomaticomaxillary buttress. Look for tenderness, step deformities, mobility, crepitus.
Mouth Opening: Reduced opening may occur because fractured zygomatic arch impinges on coronoid process, or due to pain. Measure inter-incisal opening.
Infraorbital Nerve: Test sensation of lower eyelid, cheek, side of nose, upper lip. Reduced sensation common but may recover gradually over months. Document carefully.

Investigations
CT Facial Bones: Investigation of choice. Assess: degree of displacement, orbital floor involvement, zygomatic arch, frontozygomatic suture, maxillary buttress, associated facial fractures. Review CT yourself before discussing with registrar.

Conservative Management
Many minimally displaced fractures managed without surgery. Typical features: normal facial contour, no diplopia, no significant enophthalmos, minimal displacement, adequate mouth opening. Management: analgesia, soft diet, avoidance of further trauma, facial trauma clinic follow-up.

Operative Management
Common indications: significant cosmetic flattening, persistent diplopia due to fracture displacement, clinically significant enophthalmos, reduced mouth opening from arch impingement, marked displacement, associated orbital reconstruction. Most repairs = ORIF with titanium plates/screws. Number/position of fixation points depends on pattern/stability.

Orbital Floor Involvement
Many ZMC fractures include orbital floor component. Surgical repair may be required if: persistent diplopia, muscle entrapment, significant enophthalmos, large orbital floor defect. Always discuss orbital findings with registrar.

Antibiotics
Routine antibiotics NOT indicated for isolated closed ZMC fractures. Follow local protocols if: open fractures, associated sinus injuries, surgical intervention.

Admission
Consider if: significant ocular injury, associated facial fractures, poor oral intake, uncontrolled pain, requirement for surgery, social concerns.

Discharge Advice
Advise: soft diet if chewing painful, avoid contact sports until reviewed, avoid further facial trauma, attend follow-up, return immediately if vision deteriorates or new diplopia develops. If orbital floor fracture present, advise NOT to blow nose — may precipitate orbital emphysema.

items: Every ZMC fracture requires documented eye exam — vision, movements, diplopia, globe position
Assess infraorbital nerve function in every case — medicolegal and prognostic importance
Restricted mouth opening may indicate zygomatic arch impingement — not just pain/trismus
Operate on function and deformity, not simply CT appearance — displacement alone isn’t indication

Diplopia on upward gaze only, EOM full. No enophthalmos. Reduced sensation left V2. Mouth opening 22mm due to pain. CT: displaced left ZMC with orbital floor involvement. No muscle entrapment. Impression: ZMC # with functional deficit. Plan: discuss ORIF vs conservative, ophthalmology review pending.”

title: Le Fort Fractures
quote: Le Fort fractures are not simply patterns on a CT scan—they represent instability of the midface. Always assess airway, occlusion and maxillary mobility before worrying about the classification.

items:
Why This Module Matters
Le Fort fractures are high-energy injuries involving separation of the maxilla from the facial skeleton. Most commonly seen following RTCs, significant falls, industrial accidents and major assaults. Although classically divided into Le Fort I, II and III, most modern injuries are combinations rather than “pure” patterns. For the OMFS DCT, recognising a Le Fort fracture is less important than recognising what it means: the patient has sustained major facial trauma, the airway may deteriorate rapidly, there may be associated cranial, cervical and ocular injuries, occlusion is frequently disrupted, and definitive treatment usually requires operative fixation. Your role: identify the injury, recognise associated life-threatening problems, ensure appropriate escalation.

sections.heading: Golden Rule
items: If the upper jaw moves independently from the rest of the face, think Le Fort fracture. Maxillary mobility is an important clinical finding but should only be assessed gently and once, as repeated manipulation is painful and may worsen bleeding.

sections.heading: Core Content
items:
BEFORE YOU PHONE YOUR REGISTRAR
Know: □ Mechanism of injury?, □ Airway stable?, □ Visual acuity?, □ Any diplopia?, □ Is the maxilla mobile?, □ Is the occlusion altered?, □ Is there a CSF leak?, □ Are there associated mandibular fractures?, □ CT findings?, □ Is neurosurgical or ophthalmology input required?

Understanding Le Fort Fractures
René Le Fort described predictable fracture patterns following blunt facial trauma. Useful for communication, but remember: real trauma rarely follows textbook lines. Patients often have mixed injury patterns.

Initial Assessment – ATLS Principles
Airway: Priority. Compromise may result from posterior displacement of maxilla, bleeding, loose teeth, vomiting, soft tissue swelling. Manage per trauma protocols.
Breathing: RR, SpO2, chest injuries.
Circulation: Pulse, BP, active facial bleeding. Control haemorrhage with direct pressure where appropriate.
Disability: GCS, pupils, head injury symptoms. Always consider traumatic brain injury.
Exposure: Inspect entire patient. Le Fort fractures rarely occur in isolation.

History
Mechanism: High-energy implied. RTC, fall from height, assault with weapon.
LOC/Vomiting/Amnesia: Suggests head injury.
Visual symptoms: Blurred vision, double vision.
Altered bite: New malocclusion.
Loose upper teeth: Maxillary mobility.
Facial numbness: V2 distribution.
Clear nasal discharge: Unilateral watery rhinorrhoea post-trauma raises concern for CSF leak.

Examination
Inspection: Facial swelling, bilateral periorbital bruising (raccoon eyes), epistaxis, nasal deformity, midface flattening, facial asymmetry, lacerations.
Eye Examination: Mandatory. Document VA each eye, pupils + RAPD, eye movements, diplopia, globe position. Do not omit.
Occlusion: Ask patient to bite together. Look for anterior open bite, posterior premature contacts, crossbite, new malocclusion. Document carefully.
Maxillary Mobility: Only after excluding significant C-spine concerns. Gloved hands: stabilise forehead, gently grasp upper incisors, assess abnormal movement. Do this ONCE. Repeated examination unnecessary and harmful.
Cranial Nerves: V2 — reduced sensation cheek, upper lip, side of nose. Facial nerve if soft tissue injuries.
Associated Injuries: Always look for orbital, ZMC, nasal, mandibular, skull base, C-spine fractures. Finding one facial fracture should prompt search for others.

Red Flags 🚩
Urgent senior/anaesthetics/neurosurgery/ophthalmology review if: airway threatened, visual loss, RAPD, globe rupture, retrobulbar haemorrhage, CSF rhinorrhoea, uncontrolled epistaxis, GCS drop, significant displacement, bilateral mandibular fractures, polytrauma.

CSF Leak
Suspect if: clear unilateral rhinorrhoea, persistent watery nasal discharge, salty taste, associated skull base fracture. Test: halo sign, glucose positive, beta-2 transferrin. Management: avoid nasal instrumentation, no NG tubes via nose until senior review, nurse 30° head up, discuss immediately with reg/neurosurgery. Prophylactic antibiotics controversial — follow local protocol.

Investigations
CT Facial Bones: Investigation of choice. Assess fracture pattern, maxillary displacement, orbital involvement, skull base extension, associated facial fractures. Review images yourself before discussion.
Additional Imaging: CT Head, CT C-spine, CT Angiography if vascular injury suspected. Trauma series as per ATLS.

Initial Management
Airway protection: Definitive airway if compromised. Maxillofacial injuries may require surgical airway.
Analgesia: Adequate early.
Haemorrhage control: Direct pressure, anterior/posterior nasal packs if required, consider interventional radiology for refractory epistaxis.
Soft diet/NBM: If surgery anticipated, keep NBM.
Careful oral hygiene: Chlorhexidine mouthwash if able.
Antibiotics: Most Le Fort fractures communicate with oral cavity → open fractures. Antibiotic use varies — follow local OMFS protocols.

Definitive Management
Most displaced Le Fort fractures require: open reduction, internal fixation using titanium plates, restoration of occlusion, reconstruction of facial buttresses. Precise surgical approach depends on fracture configuration. Managed via MDT with maxillofacial, neurosurgery, ophthalmology, ICU.

Admission
Nearly all true Le Fort fractures require admission. Reasons: high-energy mechanism, airway observation, operative planning, associated injuries, requirement for multidisciplinary management.

items: Occlusion is one of the most useful clinical signs — anterior open bite is classic

sections.heading: Key Takeaways
items: Le Fort fractures are high-energy injuries — always perform full trauma assessment first
Document vision and ocular findings in every patient — VA, pupils, EOM, diplopia

sections.heading: Assess occlusion and maxillary mobility carefully — single gentle examination
items: Look actively for associated facial, cranial and cervical injuries — they rarely occur alone
Most displaced Le Fort fractures require admission and operative management — airway + fixation

Registrar Handover Prompt
Lead with function not classification: “High-energy RTC. Airway patent, C-spine cleared. VA 6/6 bilaterally, no RAPD, no diplopia. Anterior open bite, maxilla mobile on gentle testing. V2 paraesthesia bilaterally. CT: Le Fort II pattern with orbital floor involvement, no skull base fracture seen. No CSF leak. Plan: admit, NBM, IV abx per protocol, theatre for ORIF, neurosurgery aware.”
Avoid: “He’s got a Le Fort II.” Focus on what matters: airway, vision, occlusion, stability, associated injuries.

title: Nasal Fractures and Septal Haematoma
quote: A nasal fracture rarely threatens the patient. A missed septal haematoma can permanently damage the nose. Always look inside before looking outside.

items:
Why This Matters
Nasal fractures are the commonest facial bone fracture. Most are isolated, low-energy injuries managed in outpatients. They rarely cause airway compromise or life-threatening bleeding. However, one complication must never be missed: septal haematoma. If unrecognised, it leads to septal cartilage necrosis, septal perforation, and saddle-nose deformity — a permanent cosmetic and functional problem. The OMFS DCT must differentiate simple nasal fracture from injuries requiring urgent drainage, and screen for associated facial/C-spine/head injuries. Your job: control bleeding, exclude septal haematoma, document function, safety-net, and refer appropriately.

sections.heading: Golden Rule
items: Always look inside the nose. The septum matters more than the dorsum. A missed septal haematoma is indefensible.

sections.heading: Core Content
items:
BEFORE YOU PHONE YOUR REGISTRAR
Know: □ Mechanism of injury?, □ Epistaxis controlled?, □ Nasal airway patent?, □ Septal haematoma present?, □ External deformity?, □ Crepitus?, □ Other facial fractures?, □ Head injury symptoms?, □ C-spine cleared?, □ Tetanus status?

Initial Assessment – ATLS Principles
Nasal fractures are usually isolated, but high-energy mechanisms require full trauma assessment.
Airway: Usually patent. Severe bilateral fractures + gross swelling can compromise airway. Blood in oropharynx → nausea/vomiting.
Breathing: RR, SpO2. Chest injuries if high-energy.
Circulation: Profuse epistaxis can cause hypotension, especially elderly/anticoagulated. Control bleeding first.
Disability: GCS, pupils, LOC, vomiting, amnesia. Head injury common with nasal #.
Exposure: Check for other facial lacerations, dental trauma, ocular injuries, C-spine tenderness.

History
Mechanism: Punch, fall, sport, RTC, assault. High-energy = screen for other injuries.
Nasal symptoms: Epistaxis — how long, one or both nostrils, soaked towels? Nasal obstruction — immediate or delayed? Change in shape — patient often best judge.
Pain: Over bridge, worse on palpation.
Previous nasal injury/surgery: Baseline deformity? Previous septoplasty/rhinoplasty affects management.
Associated: Visual disturbance, diplopia, infraorbital numbness, dental pain, CSF rhinorrhoea.

Examination
External: Swelling, bruising, lacerations, deviation, dorsal depression, telecanthus. Assess from front and bird’s-eye view. Palpate: tenderness, crepitus, step deformity, mobility. Check bony and cartilaginous dorsum.
Internal: Essential. Use headlight + Thudicum speculum or otoscope. Inspect septum for:
Septal haematoma: Bilateral, boggy, bluish swelling of septum. Soft fluctuant mass occluding airway. May be subtle early.
Septal deviation: New vs old.
Lacerations: Source of bleeding.

Foreign body: Tooth fragments, glass.
Other: Check eyes — VA, pupils, EOM, diplopia. Check occlusion — nasal # rarely alone if high-energy. Check infraorbital nerve.

Septal Haematoma – The Must-Not-Miss
Pathophysiology: Blood collects between septal cartilage and mucoperichondrium → pressure necrosis of avascular cartilage → collapse in 3–7 days → saddle-nose deformity + septal perforation.
Signs: Nasal obstruction out of proportion to external swelling, bilateral soft swelling of septum, may be red/blue. Unilateral can occur but rare.
Management: Needs urgent drainage + nasal packing + antibiotics. ENT emergency if OMFS not comfortable. Do not discharge a septal haematoma.
Red flag phrase: “My nose feels blocked and it’s getting worse.”

sections.heading:
Epistaxis Control
Most stops with simple measures:
items: Sit patient forward, pinch soft part of nose 10–15 min.
Ice pack to bridge.
If fails: topical vasoconstrictor + LA spray, silver nitrate cautery if bleeding point seen.
Anterior nasal pack: Merocel/RapidRhino. Bilateral if needed.
Posterior pack or Foley catheter if posterior bleed.
Consider coagulopathy, anticoagulants, BP control.
ENT/OMFS if uncontrolled, balloon tamponade, IR embolisation, theatre.

Red Flags 🚩
Urgent senior/ENT review if: septal haematoma, uncontrolled epistaxis, CSF rhinorrhoea, decreased VA, diplopia, enophthalmos, suspected orbital injury, telecanthus, C-spine concerns, severe deformity in child, open fracture with exposed cartilage/bone.

Investigations
X-rays: Not routinely required for simple nasal fractures. Poor sensitivity, do not change management. 
CT Facial Bones: If suspected other facial fractures, severe deformity, high-energy mechanism, orbital signs, CSF leak, child with significant trauma.
Photographs: Medicolegal + baseline. Always take with consent if deformity present.

sections.heading:
Management
Isolated Nasal Fracture, No Septal Haematoma:
items: Acute: Control bleeding, analgesia, ice, head elevation. Advise against nose blowing. Most not reduced acutely due to swelling.
Referral: ENT/OMFS clinic 5–7 days when swelling settles. MUA ± septoplasty if functional/cosmetic deformity. Patient decides.
Antibiotics: Not routine. Consider if open wound, packing in situ, or per local protocol.
Tetanus: Update if dirty wound.

sections.heading: Septal Haematoma:
items: Urgent drainage: Needle aspiration or incision + drainage under LA.
Packing: Bilateral nasal packs to prevent re-accumulation.
Antibiotics: Cover Staph/Strep per local guidelines due to risk of abscess.
Admit: Usually 24–48h observation. ENT follow-up.

sections.heading: Discharge Advice
items: No contact sports 6 weeks.
No nose blowing 2 weeks.
Sleep head elevated.
Analgesia.
Return if: worsening nasal obstruction, fever, vision changes, severe headache, clear nasal discharge, recurrent bleeding.
Warn swelling will worsen days 1–3 before improving.
Explain that final cosmetic result assessed after swelling settles — 7–10 days.

Admission Criteria
Rare. Consider if: uncontrolled epistaxis, septal haematoma, associated facial/head injury, airway concerns, social concerns, paediatric with significant trauma, need for GA.

sections.heading: Child + nasal trauma + no external swelling = think septal haematoma
items: Most litigation in nasal trauma comes from missed septal haematoma, not missed reduction

sections.heading: Key Takeaways
items: Always examine inside the nose — septal haematoma is the complication that matters
Epistaxis management: pressure, cautery, pack, escalate. Don’t send home bleeding

sections.heading: Safety-net: worsening obstruction, vision changes, CSF leak, fever → return
items:
Registrar Handover Prompt
Structure: Mechanism, epistaxis controlled?, septal haematoma excluded?, deformity, other injuries, plan.
“22M punched. No LOC, C-spine cleared. Epistaxis stopped with 10min pressure. No septal haematoma on speculum exam. External swelling, dorsal deviation R. VA normal, no diplopia. No other facial #. Plan: discharge with nasal fracture advice, ENT clinic 1/52, safety-netted.”
Red flag version: “5yo fall. Nasal obstruction worsening. Bilateral boggy septum — septal haematoma. Needs ENT now for drainage.”

sections.heading: Exclude septal haematoma — use headlight + speculum
items:
Document vision — even if “unrelated”
Miss septal haematoma and the patient gets a permanent deformity. Miss bleeding and they re-attend. Miss vision and you miss orbital injury.

title: Facial Lacerations
quote: A well-repaired facial laceration may be almost invisible in a year's time. A poorly repaired one may be remembered for life. Good technique begins with good assessment.

items:
Why This Module Matters
Facial lacerations account for a significant proportion of OMFS emergency referrals. Although many appear straightforward, they often coexist with facial fractures, dental injuries, nerve injuries, salivary duct injuries or ocular trauma. The cosmetic and functional consequences of poor management can last a lifetime. Repairing facial lacerations is one of the first practical skills you will develop as an OMFS DCT. Success depends far less on suturing technique than on your ability to assess the wound properly, handle tissues gently and restore normal anatomy. Remember: The operation starts the moment you examine the wound—not when you pick up the needle holder.

sections.heading: Golden Rule
items: Never close a wound until you know what lies beneath it. Every facial laceration should be considered a potential injury to deeper structures until proven otherwise.

sections.heading: Core Content
items:
BEFORE YOU PHONE YOUR REGISTRAR
Know: □ Mechanism of injury?, □ Is there underlying fracture?, □ Is there facial nerve injury?, □ Is parotid duct intact?, □ Is there tissue loss?, □ Is wound contaminated?, □ Is eyelid, lip or nose involved?, □ Tetanus status?, □ Does this require theatre?

Initial Assessment
Always perform ABCDE before concentrating on the wound. Large facial lacerations can be distracting. Do not miss: airway compromise, C-spine injury, head injury, major haemorrhage, ocular injury.

History
Mechanism: Fall, assault, glass, knife, animal bite, RTC, sport. Mechanism predicts contamination and underlying injury.
Timing: Exact time of injury, any previous attempts at closure.
Symptoms: Facial numbness, weakness, double vision, difficulty chewing, difficulty closing eye, altered bite. These suggest injuries beyond skin.

Examination
Step 1 – Control Bleeding: Direct pressure, LA with adrenaline where appropriate, haemostatic measures if required. Avoid immediately placing sutures into bleeding wound. Good haemostasis improves visibility enormously.
Step 2 – Clean the Wound: Before deciding closure: remove dirt, gravel, glass, tooth fragments, clothing fibres. Copious irrigation with normal saline is one of the most important parts of wound management. The solution to pollution is dilution.
Step 3 – Examine Properly: Assess length, depth, tissue loss, contamination, devitalised tissue, foreign bodies. Good lighting essential.

Look for Underlying Injuries
Never assume a laceration is "just a cut." Specifically assess for: facial fractures, dental injuries, parotid duct injury, facial nerve injury, globe injury, lacrimal system injury, cartilage exposure, muscle injury.

Facial Nerve Examination
Any wound over parotid or cheek prompts facial nerve exam. Ask patient to: raise eyebrows, close eyes tightly, smile, puff out cheeks, show teeth. Document findings BEFORE local anaesthetic if possible.

Parotid Duct Injury
Suspect if wound crosses line joining tragus to midpoint of upper lip. Signs: saliva leaking into wound, difficulty expressing saliva into mouth. These injuries require senior review. Consider probing or sialography per local protocol.

sections.heading: Specialised Structures
items:
Choosing Local Anaesthetic
Common: Lidocaine 1% with adrenaline, Lidocaine 2%, Bupivacaine for prolonged analgesia. Adrenaline provides better haemostasis, visibility, longer anaesthesia. Avoid intravascular injection. Always aspirate. Avoid adrenaline in end arteries — fingers, penis — but face is safe.

sections.heading: Suture Selection
items: Follow local consultant preference.

Principles of Wound Closure
Based on: gentle tissue handling, anatomical alignment, layered closure, minimal tension, accurate skin edge approximation, slight wound edge eversion. Do not strangulate tissues with overly tight knots.

Layered Closure
Close from deep to superficial: 1. Muscle 2. Deep dermis 3. Skin. Eliminate dead space where possible.

Dog Ears
Minor standing cones often flatten with time. Do not aggressively excise normal tissue to achieve immediate perfection.

Tissue Loss
If tissue loss prevents tension-free closure: do NOT force wound together. Discuss with registrar. Skin grafts or local flaps may be required.

Red Flags 🚩
Escalate immediately: facial nerve weakness, parotid duct injury, lid margin/canaliculus involvement, globe injury, cartilage exposure with inadequate cover, human/animal bite, gross contamination, delayed presentation >24h with infection, underlying fracture.

Antibiotics
Routine antibiotics NOT required for every facial laceration. Consider when: animal/human bite, gross contamination, open fracture, cartilage involvement, delayed presentation, immunocompromise. Follow local antimicrobial guidance.

Tetanus
Always assess tetanus status. Follow national guidance regarding boosters and immunoglobulin where indicated.

Dressing
Most facial wounds: simple non-adherent dressing for 24h. Some left uncovered. Avoid bulky dressings over face where possible.

sections.heading: Suture Removal
items:
Scar Advice
Advise: keep wound clean, protect from sunlight 12+ months, SPF 50 sunscreen, silicone gel once epithelialised, gentle scar massage after healing. Explain scars mature for up to 1 year.

items: Examine before you anaesthetise and anaesthetise before you suture — nerve function must be documented pre-LA

sections.heading: Copious irrigation is one of the most important parts of wound management
items: Always assess facial nerve function before closure when wound is over cheek/parotid region

sections.heading: Vermilion border is the most important landmark in lip repair — align it first
items: Good cosmetic outcomes depend on assessment, layered closure, meticulous handling — not more stitches

No #, facial nerve intact pre-LA. No parotid duct leak on testing. Clean, no tissue loss. Plan LA + layered closure 6-0 Prolene. Tetanus up to date. Would I be happy if this scar were on my own face?

title: Human and Animal Bite Injuries
quote: Bite wounds may look small on the surface, but they are contaminated injuries with a high risk of infection. Respect every bite, irrigate it thoroughly and never underestimate what lies beneath the skin.

items:
Why This Module Matters
Bite injuries are common OMFS/ED presentations. Human and animal mouths contain polymicrobial flora with high pathogenic potential. Human bites have higher infection rates than dog bites due to Eikenella, Strep, Staph, anaerobes, and viral risk. Cat bites cause deep puncture wounds with Pasteurella multocida → rapid cellulitis/septic arthritis. Small skin wounds often hide significant deep tissue damage, devitalised tissue, or foreign bodies like teeth. Delayed presentation, inadequate irrigation, and premature closure cause abscess, osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, and systemic infection. Rabies, tetanus, hepatitis B/C, and HIV must be considered. Your role: assess thoroughly, irrigate aggressively, debride devitalised tissue, decide on closure vs delayed closure, give prophylaxis, and safety-net.

sections.heading: Golden Rule
items: Every bite is contaminated. Irrigation and debridement are more important than antibiotics. Never close a high-risk bite primarily without senior discussion.

sections.heading: Core Content
items:
BEFORE YOU PHONE YOUR REGISTRAR
Know: □ Human or animal?, □ Time since injury?, □ Site + depth?, □ Tendon/joint/bone/cartilage involved?, □ Neurovascular status distal?, □ Signs of infection?, □ Immunisation status?, □ Rabies risk?, □ Antibiotic given?, □ Needs theatre?

sections.heading:
Classification
By Source:
items: Human: Occlusional bites, clenched-fist injuries/“fight bite” over MCPJ, love bites, paediatric. Highest infection rate 10–50%. Risk: Eikenella corrodens, Strep, Staph aureus, anaerobes, Hep B/C, HIV, HSV.
Dog: Crush + tear + puncture. Large breeds = tissue loss. Risk: Pasteurella, Staph, Strep, Capnocytophaga, anaerobes. Rabies risk depends on geography/animal status.
Cat: Puncture wounds. Small surface wound, deep inoculation. Pasteurella multocida → rapid progression <24h. High risk septic arthritis/osteomyelitis.
Other: Bats, monkeys, rodents. Rabies + specific organisms.

By Timing:
<6–8 hours: “Golden period” for washout. Lower infection risk.

8–24 hours: High infection risk. Delayed primary closure or leave open.
24 hours: Infected by definition. Do not close primarily.

Initial Assessment – ABCDE
Most isolated bites are not life-threatening, but assess airway if facial/neck bites, breathing if chest bites, circulation if major vessel involved. Check for shock in extensive bites or paediatrics.

History
Mechanism: Provoked/unprovoked, domestic/wild/stray animal, known human, circumstances. Unprovoked animal attack raises rabies concern.
Time: Exact time of injury — determines closure options and prophylaxis windows.
Animal status: Vaccinated, behaviour, quarantined, location for bats.
Patient factors: Diabetes, immunosuppression, asplenia, liver disease, prosthetic joints, PVD — all increase infection risk.
First aid: Was wound washed? Antibiotics already given?
Tetanus: Last dose, number of doses.
BBV risk: Human bites — Hep B status of patient + assailant, HIV risk, last sexual health screen.

Examination
General: Temp, pulse, BP. Sepsis? Distressed child?
Wound: Site, size, depth, shape, edges. Puncture vs laceration vs avulsion. Crushing? Devitalised tissue?
Explore: Under LA and good light. Must see base. Assess through full range of movement — tendon injuries hidden when static. Look for foreign bodies: tooth fragments, debris.
Deep structures: Tendon — loss of function, tenosynovitis. Joint — penetrate capsule? Bone — fracture, tooth marks on bone. Nerve — sensation distal. Vessel — cap refill, Doppler. Cartilage — ear/nose lacerations.
Infection: Erythema, warmth, swelling, purulent discharge, lymphangitis, lymphadenopathy, fever, spreading cellulitis.
Hand bites: Always assume joint/tendon involvement until proven otherwise. “Fight bite” over MCPJ = septic arthritis risk. XR for foreign body and air in joint.

Red Flags 🚩
Urgent senior/theatre if: deep puncture over joint/tendon/bone, crush injury with devitalised tissue, signs of infection, systemic illness, functional deficit, nerve/artery injury, facial bites with cosmetic/functional concern, ear/nose cartilage involvement, child, immunocompromised, delayed presentation >24h, human bite to hand, suspected fracture.

Investigations
X-ray: If suspected fracture, joint penetration, foreign body, tooth fragment. Clenched-fist injury — XR MCPJ.
USS: Consider for deep collection/abscess.
CT: If extensive facial bite, bony involvement, deep neck spaces.
Bloods: FBC, CRP, U&E if infected/systemically unwell, admission likely. Blood cultures if febrile.
Swabs: Take from deep tissue/pus for MC&S before antibiotics if infected. Routine swab of fresh wound low yield.
Viral: Human bite — consider Hep B, Hep C, HIV serology baseline + follow-up per local protocol. Risk assess for PEP.

Management
Step 1 – Irrigation: Copious irrigation is most important. Use sterile saline under pressure — 19G needle + 50ml syringe, or pulse lavage. Minimum 250–500ml per wound. More for deep/contaminated.
Step 2 – Debridement: Excise all devitalised tissue, clot, foreign material. Explore to base. Extend wound if needed for access. Do not leave necrotic tissue.
Step 3 – Closure: Decision depends on time, site, contamination, species.
Primary closure: Clean, <8h old, face/scalp for cosmesis, not hands/feet/joints, after thorough washout. Always discuss facial bites with senior.
Delayed primary closure: 3–5 days, high-risk wounds after initial washout + packing.

Healing by secondary intention: Heavily contaminated, >24h old, puncture wounds, hands, feet, immunocompromised. Pack and review.
Step 4 – Antibiotics: Prophylaxis indicated for most bite wounds. Cover Pasteurella, Staph, Strep, anaerobes. Follow local guidelines. Typical: co-amoxiclav PO/IV. Penicillin allergy: doxycycline + metronidazole or clindamycin + ciprofloxacin per local policy. Duration: 3–5 days prophylaxis, 7–14 days if infected.
Step 5 – Tetanus: Assess status. Clean wound + fully immunised <10y ago = none. Tetanus-prone wound or >10y = booster. If unknown/incomplete, give vaccine ± immunoglobulin per national guidance.
Step 6 – Rabies: Risk assess per UKHSA algorithm. Bite from bat, or terrestrial mammal in endemic country. Post-exposure prophylaxis = vaccine ± HRIG depending on category. Discuss with virology/ID. Do not delay.
Step 7 – BBV: Human bites. Risk assess for Hep B PEP/vaccine, Hep C follow-up, HIV PEP if high-risk. Baseline serology for patient. Document discussion.
Step 8 – Elevation: Especially hand injuries. Reduces oedema/infection.
Step 9 – Follow-up: Review 24–48h for high-risk wounds. Hands need hand surgery review. Facial wounds need OMFS/plastics follow-up.

Specific Scenarios
Human bite to hand / Fight bite: Always assume joint penetration. XR, washout in theatre, splint, IV antibiotics, admit. High risk septic arthritis.
Cat bite: Early antibiotics even if looks clean. Pasteurella progresses rapidly. Low threshold for admission.
Facial bite: Cosmetic + functional importance. Washout + delayed primary closure common. Discuss with senior/plastics. Avoid closing if infected.
Ear/nose: Cartilage involved = high infection risk. Debride carefully, avoid suturing through cartilage, bolsters, ENT/OMFS input.
Child: Non-accidental injury must be considered. Paediatric safeguarding if concerns. Dog bites to face common.

Admission Criteria
Systemic infection, spreading cellulitis, deep structure involvement, need for GA washout, facial bite requiring specialist closure, immunocompromised, failed outpatient treatment, poor compliance, safeguarding concerns.
