□ Human or animal + circumstances
□ Time since injury
□ Site, depth, structures involved
□ Neurovascular status
□ Signs of infection
□ Irrigation done?
□ X-ray if indicated
□ Tetanus status
□ Rabies/BBV risk assessed
□ Plan: closure vs open, antibiotics given, admission needed?

sections.heading: Puncture wounds are worse than they look — cat bites especially
items: Fight bites are never “just a laceration” — joint is involved until proven otherwise

sections.heading: Key Takeaways
items: All bites are contaminated — irrigate aggressively and debride devitalised tissue
Do not close high-risk wounds primarily — hands, feet, punctures, >8–24h, infected, immunocompromised

sections.heading: Consider tetanus, rabies, Hep B/C, HIV — risk assess every bite
items: Low threshold for senior review/theatre — especially hands, face, joints, children

Registrar Handover Prompt
Structure: species, time, site, depth, structures, infection, neurovascular, irrigation done, XR, tetanus/rabies/BBV, plan.
“Dog bite 2h ago to L cheek, 3cm laceration, no deep structure involved, neurovascular intact. Irrigated 500ml saline, no foreign body. Tetanus up to date, dog vaccinated UK, no rabies risk. Plan: delayed primary closure in AM, co-amoxiclav, OMFS clinic 48h.”
Red flag: “Human fight bite to R hand MCPJ 12h ago. Swelling, pain on movement, XR shows air in joint. For theatre washout, IV co-amoxiclav, elevate, hand surgery referral.”

sections.heading: Don’t close high-risk wounds — hands, punctures, late, dirty
items:
Prophylaxis — antibiotics + tetanus + consider rabies/BBV
If you do these four, you prevent most complications.

title: Facial Skin and Soft Tissue Abscesses
quote: Where there is pus, it usually needs drainage. Antibiotics alone rarely cure a mature abscess. Your job is to recognise when a facial infection has become a surgical problem.

items:
Why This Module Matters
Not every facial swelling is dental in origin. OMFS teams frequently assess facial skin and soft tissue infections: infected epidermoid (sebaceous) cysts, infected traumatic wounds, post-op wound infections, infected haematomas, cellulitis, spontaneous facial abscesses. Most are straightforward, but some are rapidly progressive infections requiring urgent surgery, while others may be infected malignancies or deep fascial space infections masquerading as superficial swellings. Your role: differentiate cellulitis from abscess, identify patients suitable for LA drainage, recognise when admission/theatre required, exclude underlying pathology, escalate early when infection spreading or patient systemically unwell.

sections.heading: Golden Rule
items: Drain the pus—but always ask why it formed. A facial abscess is often secondary to an underlying problem that also requires treatment.

sections.heading: Core Content
items:
BEFORE YOU PHONE YOUR REGISTRAR
Know: □ Where is the swelling?, □ Cellulitis or abscess?, □ Is there fluctuance?, □ Is there overlying skin necrosis?, □ Any facial nerve weakness?, □ Is patient systemically unwell?, □ Previous similar episodes?, □ History of skin cancer or previous surgery?, □ Blood results?, □ Ultrasound or CT required?

Common Causes
Facial soft tissue abscesses commonly arise from: infected epidermoid (sebaceous) cysts, infected traumatic wounds, post-operative wound infections, infected haematomas, folliculitis/furunculosis, infected skin lesions, insect bites, foreign bodies, salivary gland infections (covered separately). Not every fluctuant swelling is "just a cyst."

sections.heading: Cellulitis vs Abscess
items:
History
Ask: duration, rapid progression, previous episodes, recent trauma, previous surgery, skin lesions, insect bites, diabetes, immunosuppression, MRSA history, fever/rigors. Recurrent abscesses → consider underlying cyst, foreign body, or immunocompromised state.

Examination
Inspect: Site, size, skin colour, necrosis, pointing, previous scars, sinus formation.
Palpate: Fluctuance, induration, tenderness, crepitus, regional lymphadenopathy.
Always assess: Surrounding tissues. A small abscess may be surrounded by extensive cellulitis.
Facial nerve: Document CN VII function before any intervention. Weakness changes management urgently.

Red Flags 🚩
Urgent senior review if: rapid progression, significant facial swelling affecting eye, facial nerve weakness, skin necrosis, crepitus, severe systemic illness, failure to improve on antibiotics, immunocompromise, suspicion of necrotising soft tissue infection.

Necrotising Soft Tissue Infection
Rare but must consider. Features: pain out of proportion, rapid progression, skin discolouration, bullae, crepitus, systemic toxicity. Surgical emergency. Escalate immediately — do not wait for imaging or abx response.

Investigations
Bloods: FBC, CRP, U&E, blood cultures if septic.
Ultrasound: Useful for distinguishing cellulitis from abscess, identifying superficial collections, guiding aspiration.
CT with Contrast: If infection extensive, deep extension suspected, orbital involvement, uncertain diagnosis, recurrent infection, failure of treatment.

Incision and Drainage – Principles
Indications: Fluctuance, pointing, imaging-confirmed collection, failure of antibiotics.
Incision planning: Follow relaxed skin tension lines where possible. Large enough for adequate drainage. Avoid important aesthetic subunits where possible. Respect facial nerve branches — lies immediately deep to SMAS in many areas.
Technique: LA, prep, incise, send pus for MC&S where appropriate, break down loculations with artery forceps, irrigate copiously, consider small drain or ribbon gauze.
Key point: A tiny incision into a large abscess rarely works.

Antibiotics
Indicated for: associated cellulitis, systemic features, immunocompromised, extensive surrounding inflammation. Routine antibiotics NOT always necessary after complete drainage of small uncomplicated abscess in well patient. Follow local antimicrobial guidance.

When Should You Worry?
Consider alternative diagnoses if: swelling hard rather than fluctuant, recurrent infections at same site, delayed healing, lesion ulcerated, unexplained tissue loss, history of skin cancer. An infected skin malignancy can mimic abscess. Do not excise suspected malignancy without senior input.

sections.heading: Consultant Pearls 💡
items: Most recurrent facial abscesses arise from underlying epidermoid cyst — excise formally once infection settled
Avoid excising infected cyst during acute phase unless consultant advises — inflamed planes make complete excision difficult, recurrence likely

sections.heading: Always consider underlying cause — cyst, foreign body, malignancy, haematoma
items: Do not attempt formal cyst excision during acute infection — I&D first, excise later
Respect facial nerve anatomy — document function pre-op, plan incision carefully
Never dismiss recurrent/atypical lesions — infected SCC/BCC presents as “abscess”

Registrar Handover Checklist
Before calling: □ Site of abscess, □ Cellulitis or abscess?, □ Size, □ Fluctuance, □ Facial nerve exam, □ Systemic obs, □ Blood results, □ Imaging findings, □ Antibiotics given, □ Whether drainage performed or required.

sections.heading: Will my incision follow relaxed skin tension lines?
items:
Does this patient actually need theatre instead of LA drainage?
Good surgery begins before the scalpel touches the skin.

Clinical Pearl – The Consultant's Question
If asked: "Why does this patient keep getting the same abscess?"
Good answer: "The infection is likely secondary to an underlying epidermoid cyst or retained foreign body. Drainage treats the acute infection, but definitive management requires addressing the underlying pathology once inflammation has resolved." Treating abscess alone without removing cause leads to recurrence.

title: Salivary Gland Emergencies
quote: A painful swollen salivary gland is usually obstructed until proven otherwise. Your job is to distinguish obstruction, infection and abscess formation from neoplasia.

items:
Why This Module Matters
Acute salivary gland swellings are core OMFS on-call work. Most are due to obstruction by sialoliths leading to stasis and secondary bacterial infection. The spectrum is wide: mild sialadenitis resolving with hydration, through to deep neck space abscesses and Ludwig’s angina that threaten airway. Neoplasia can mimic acute inflammation. Your job: identify the gland, assess airway/sepsis fast, decide if obstruction/infection/abscess, and know when admission or theatre is needed. Ludwig’s angina kills by airway obstruction, not sepsis — miss this and the patient dies.

sections.heading: Golden Rule
items: Sudden painful swelling of a salivary gland on eating is a stone until proven otherwise. Bilateral floor of mouth swelling + tongue elevation = airway emergency — act now, image later.

sections.heading: Core Content
items:
BEFORE YOU PHONE YOUR REGISTRAR
Know: □ Which gland + side?, □ Onset with eating?, □ Pus from duct?, □ Stone palpable?, □ Trismus in mm?, □ Dysphagia/voice change/drooling?, □ Floor of mouth raised?, □ Temp/NEWS2?, □ USS/CT findings?, □ Airway secured?, □ Antibiotics started?

sections.heading: Key Anatomy
items:
Initial Assessment – ABCDE
Airway: Priority. Ludwig’s angina = bilateral submandibular + sublingual + submental spaces. Signs: raised floor of mouth, tongue pushed up/back, drooling, “hot potato” voice, stridor. If present: stay with patient, sit upright, call anaesthetics + reg now. Do NOT send for CT or lie flat.
Breathing: RR, SpO2, work of breathing.
Circulation: Temp, HR, BP. Sepsis screen if NEWS2 ≥5 or looks unwell.
Disability: GCS, pain.
Exposure: Neck swelling, extent, skin erythema, trismus, cervical lymphadenopathy.

History – Key Questions
Timing: Seconds with food = stone. Hours-days worsening = infection. Weeks painless = neoplasm.
Pain: Colicky on eating = obstruction. Constant throbbing = infection/abscess.
Swelling: Intermittent = stone. Persistent + increasing = infection.
Systemic: Fever, rigors, malaise, dehydration.
PMH: Sjögren’s, HIV, previous radiotherapy, stones, anticholinergics, dehydration, diabetes, immunosuppression.
Dental: Poor OH, calculus, recent extraction.

Examination
Extraoral: Unilateral warm tender swelling over anatomical site. Bimanual palpation for submandibular gland: one finger intraoral floor of mouth, one extraoral. Stone often palpable in Wharton’s.
Intraoral: Inspect duct orifices. Look for erythema, swelling. Milk gland from posterior to anterior — pus confirms bacterial sialadenitis. Check dentition.
Trismus: Measure inter-incisal opening. <20mm suggests masticator space involvement.
Floor of Mouth: Raise tongue — if raised, woody, tender bilaterally = Ludwig’s until proven otherwise.
Cranial nerves: Facial nerve if parotid swelling — parotid malignancy can present acutely with infection.

sections.heading: Differential Diagnosis
items:
Red Flags 🚩
Immediate senior/anaesthetics if: stridor, voice change, dysphagia, drooling, tongue elevation, trismus <20mm, rapidly spreading cellulitis, sepsis, immunocompromise, failure to improve 24–48h on IV antibiotics. These suggest deep space abscess or Ludwig’s.

Investigations
Bloods: FBC, CRP, U&E, blood cultures if febrile/septic.
Pus: MC&S if expressed or drained.
Imaging:
USS: First line. Differentiates sialadenitis vs abscess vs stone. Bedside, no radiation. Can guide aspiration.
OPG: Shows 80% of submandibular stones. Quick if available.
Contrast CT neck: For Ludwig’s, trismus preventing exam, deep abscess suspicion, failed treatment, or airway concern. Shows extent + airway.
MRI: Outpatient for suspected neoplasm, not emergency.

sections.heading: Management Pathways
items:
1. Sialolithiasis + Mild Sialadenitis
Conservative: Hydration 2–3L/day, sialogogues — lemon, chewing gum, warm compress, gland massage toward orifice, analgesia, good OH. Antibiotics only if infection signs: co-amoxiclav 625mg TDS 5–7 days. Penicillin allergy: clindamycin 300mg QDS. Most small stones pass. OP follow-up for USS/sialendoscopy. Safety-net: return if fever, dysphagia, breathing issues.

2. Acute Bacterial Sialadenitis – Unwell
Admit if: unable to swallow, sepsis, large swelling, immunosuppressed. IV co-amoxiclav 1.2g TDS, IV fluids, analgesia, warm compress, massage. Reassess 24h with USS. If abscess → drainage.

3. Salivary Gland Abscess
Fluctuant, systemic illness, not settling on antibiotics. Confirm with USS. Needs drainage: intraoral if accessible, extraoral if deep parotid/submandibular. Send pus MC&S. Continue IV antibiotics 24–48h post-drainage then oral. Ludwig’s angina = bilateral spaces → theatre for wide drainage + airway.

sections.heading: 4. Ludwig’s Angina Protocol
items: Call anaesthetics + senior OMFS/ENT immediately.
Sit patient up. High-flow O2. Do NOT lie flat.
Secure airway: awake fibreoptic intubation or tracheostomy. Intubation difficult due to oedema.
CT only AFTER airway safe.
Theatre: bilateral submandibular + submental decompression.
IV antibiotics: co-amoxiclav + metronidazole, or per local severe deep neck space protocol.
ITU post-op. Mortality high if airway missed.

Antibiotics
Cover S. aureus, oral streps, anaerobes. Pasteurella not usual here.
First line: IV co-amoxiclav 1.2g TDS. PO: 625mg TDS.
Penicillin allergy: clindamycin 600mg IV TDS or 300mg PO QDS + metronidazole 400mg TDS.
Adjust to cultures. Duration: 7–14 days total depending on drainage.

Admission Criteria
Airway concern, Ludwig’s, unable to take oral meds/fluids, sepsis, abscess needing drainage, immunocompromised, failed outpatient Rx, no social support, child.

Discharge Criteria
Well, tolerating oral intake, pain controlled, no airway issues, clear plan + follow-up, safety-netted. Warn: return if swelling ↑, swallowing/breathing worse, fever persists >48h on antibiotics, trismus worsens.

DCT Checklist: Before You Phone Your Registrar
□ Which gland + side
□ Obstructive vs infective vs Ludwig’s
□ Airway: voice, swallow, FOM, trismus
□ Sepsis: temp, NEWS2
□ Pus expressed? Stone felt?
□ USS/CT findings
□ Antibiotics given
□ Airway plan if Ludwig’s
□ Admission/drainage need

sections.heading: Milk the duct — if pus comes out, diagnosis made and treatment started
items: Stone at duct orifice: consider dilating with lacrimal probe + retrieve in ED if confident
Ludwig’s = clinical diagnosis. If you suspect it, you’re probably right. Get help now

sections.heading: USS beats CT for gland itself; CT beats USS for deep neck spaces
items: Persistent unilateral gland swelling without infection >3 weeks = 2WW for cancer

sections.heading: Pus + fever = bacterial sialadenitis — antibiotics ± drainage. Admit if unwell
items: Bilateral FOM swelling + dysphagia = Ludwig’s — airway emergency, anaesthetics + theatre

sections.heading: Don’t incise suspected tumour — if hard, fixed, no infection, refer 2WW
items:
Registrar Handover Prompt
“28F, 6h R submandibular pain/swelling on eating lunch. Temp 38.1, NEWS2 2. Tender R submandibular gland, 5mm stone palpable in Wharton’s duct, pus expressed. FOM soft, no trismus, voice normal. USS: distal stone, no abscess. Impression: acute obstructive sialadenitis. Plan: IV co-amoxiclav, hydration, analgesia, milk duct. Review AM for stone removal vs conservative. Safety-netted.”

Airway version: “62M, 48h worsening bilateral submandibular swelling. Drooling, muffled voice, FOM raised and tender, tongue elevated. RR 22, SpO2 94%. Stridor absent but concerned. Impression: Ludwig’s angina. Anaesthetics + ITU called, NBM, IV co-amoxiclav + metronidazole, for emergency airway + theatre drainage.”

sections.heading:
DCT Survival Box 🚨
The Three Questions That Save Lives
items: Is the airway safe? Check voice, swallow, FOM, tongue. If no, stop and escalate.
Is it infected or just blocked? Pus + fever = infection. Meal timing = stone.

Do I need to drain or scan now? Fluctuance/trismus/systemic = USS/CT + drainage.
If airway unsafe, nothing else matters until anaesthetics are present.

DCT Survival Box 🚨 – The "5 Ms" of Salivary Gland Assessment
Before presenting any salivary gland patient, run through:

sections.heading: Meals — Does swelling worsen when eating? Stone/obstruction if yes
items: Massage — Does saliva or pus express from the duct? Pus = bacterial sialadenitis
Mass — Is it diffuse, fluctuant or a discrete lump? Diffuse = sialadenitis, fluctuant = abscess, discrete lump = ?tumour
Movement — Is facial nerve function normal? Parotid malignancy can present with facial weakness
Markers — What do inflammatory markers and imaging show? WCC/CRP ↑ = infection, USS/CT = stone vs abscess vs mass
Answer these five questions and you’ll have covered the key clinical issues in almost every salivary gland emergency.

title: Temporomandibular Joint (TMJ) Emergencies
quote: Not every patient who cannot close their mouth has a dislocated jaw—but every true TMJ dislocation should be recognised promptly, reduced safely and investigated for the underlying cause.

items:
Why This Module Matters
TMJ emergencies are relatively uncommon, but every OMFS DCT will encounter them on-call. Most are acute anterior TMJ dislocations, but referrals include condylar fractures, acute trismus, septic arthritis of the TMJ and post-op complications. Distinguishing these is essential because management differs significantly. Most acute TMJ dislocations can be reduced safely in ED with analgesia, muscle relaxation and good technique. Repeated unsuccessful attempts increase muscle spasm, making reduction harder. Your priorities: confirm diagnosis, exclude associated fractures, provide analgesia, reduce safely where appropriate, recognise when senior help/theatre required.

sections.heading: Golden Rule
items: A patient with a true bilateral TMJ dislocation cannot close their mouth—don't keep asking them to try. Once diagnosed, focus on reduction rather than repeated examination.

sections.heading: Core Content
items:
BEFORE YOU PHONE YOUR REGISTRAR
Know: □ Is this a true dislocation?, □ Any history of trauma?, □ Patient able to close mouth?, □ Is occlusion normal?, □ Previous dislocations?, □ Neurological deficit?, □ Imaging performed?, □ Reduction attempted?, □ Sedation required?, □ Is theatre likely?

Relevant Anatomy
TMJ = mandibular condyle, glenoid fossa, articular eminence, articular disc, joint capsule, muscles of mastication. Most acute dislocations are anterior — condyle trapped anterior to articular eminence. Posterior, superior, lateral dislocations rare and associated with significant trauma.

Common Presentations
Mouth locked open, inability to speak clearly, drooling, jaw pain, anxiety, difficulty swallowing saliva, preauricular discomfort. Diagnosis usually clinical.

Initial Assessment – ABCDE
Most isolated TMJ dislocations don’t compromise airway. Always ABCDE if: facial trauma, reduced GCS, polytrauma, significant bleeding. Airway can be threatened if bilateral condylar fractures with posterior displacement.

History
Mechanism: Yawning, laughing, dental treatment, vomiting, GA, seizures, facial trauma. Trauma raises suspicion for condylar fractures.
Previous Episodes: "Has this happened before?" Recurrent dislocations common in: generalised ligamentous laxity, connective tissue disorders, chronic TMJ instability.
PMH: Parkinson’s, epilepsy, connective tissue disorders, previous TMJ surgery.
Drugs: Antipsychotics → acute dystonic reaction mimics dislocation.

Examination
Inspection: Mouth persistently open, inability to occlude teeth, excess salivation, distress. Patients often support mandible with both hands.
Palpation: Preauricular region. Condyles palpable anterior to articular eminence in dislocation. Empty glenoid fossa.
Occlusion: In true anterior bilateral dislocation, patient unable to achieve occlusion. This distinguishes dislocation from many fractures.
Cranial nerves: Assess V3 sensation — inferior alveolar nerve. CN VII if trauma present.

sections.heading: Differential Diagnosis
items: History usually provides diagnosis.

Red Flags 🚩
Escalate if: trauma mechanism, suspected fracture, first presentation with uncertain diagnosis, failed reduction, persistent pain after reduction, facial nerve weakness, inability to rule out condylar fracture, systemic illness.

sections.heading:
Investigations
Imaging:
items: No imaging needed: Obvious atraumatic recurrent anterior dislocation, successful reduction, no trauma.

Imaging required: Trauma, suspicion of fracture, first presentation uncertain, failed reduction, persistent pain.
CT Facial Bones: Preferred if fracture suspected. Shows condylar position + fractures.
OPG: May show condylar position but less useful than CT in trauma. Can miss fractures.

Initial Management
Provide: analgesia — NSAIDs + paracetamol, +/- opioids. Reassurance. Quiet environment. Muscle spasm ↑ with anxiety and repeated attempts.

Manual Reduction – Principles
Must be attempted by appropriately trained clinicians.
Principle: Mandible must be depressed inferiorly to disengage condyle from articular eminence before guiding posteriorly into glenoid fossa. Movement is downwards first, then backwards. Pushing back alone fails.

sections.heading: Practical Tips:
items: Sit patient upright or slightly reclined. Support occiput against wall/chair.
Explain procedure. Get patient to relax — jaw will “drop” when muscles relax.
Adequate analgesia + muscle relaxation: consider Entonox, IV midazolam 1–2mg, or procedural sedation per local policy.
Operator: gloves, gauze over thumbs. Thumbs on mandibular molars/occlusal surface. Fingers grip inferior border mandible extraorally.
Apply firm steady pressure downwards to overcome masseter spasm, then guide posteriorly.
Be prepared to withdraw thumbs quickly — mandible snaps shut.
Bilateral: reduce one side at a time or simultaneously depending on preference.
Alternative Techniques: Conventional intraoral, wrist pivot, syringe technique for selected uncomplicated anterior dislocations, extraoral techniques. Follow local practice/consultant preference.

After Successful Reduction
Reassess: occlusion — should return to pre-morbid, mouth opening, pain, mandibular movements. Document reduction clearly: “Bilateral TMJ dislocation reduced successfully. Occlusion restored. Patient comfortable.”

sections.heading: OMFS follow-up if recurrent or first time
items: Some patients benefit from supportive bandage/Barraquer wire splint immediately post-reduction per local protocol

When Reduction Fails
Causes: muscle spasm, delayed presentation >12–24h, fracture, incorrect diagnosis, patient unable to relax. Do NOT continue repeated forceful attempts. Escalate to reg. Reduction under sedation/GA may be required. Consider LA injection to joint or muscle relaxant. If still fails → theatre.

Recurrent Dislocation
Refer for specialist assessment. Options: physiotherapy, occlusal splints selected patients, botulinum toxin to lateral pterygoid selected cases, eminectomy, Dautrey procedure, capsular plication in refractory cases.

Septic Arthritis of the TMJ
Uncommon but serious. Suspect if: fever, severe preauricular pain, trismus, swelling, raised inflammatory markers, systemically unwell. Needs urgent imaging — USS or contrast CT, IV antibiotics, senior review. May need joint aspiration/washout in theatre.

DCT Checklist: Before You Phone Your Registrar
□ Mechanism: trauma or atraumatic?
□ Previous episodes
□ Occlusion pre-reduction
□ Imaging findings if done
□ Reduction attempted? How many times?
□ Sedation used?
□ Successful reduction?
□ Persistent pain
□ Follow-up arranged

sections.heading: Consultant Pearls 💡
items: Most atraumatic anterior dislocations are clinical diagnoses — don’t CT everyone

sections.heading: Document occlusion before and after — medicolegal and functional importance
items: If patient has had GA recently, think bilateral condylar fractures not dislocation

sections.heading: Reassess and document occlusion after reduction — confirms success
items:
Registrar Handover Prompt
“23F, atraumatic bilateral TMJ dislocation after yawning. Third episode this year. No trauma, occlusion deranged, cannot close mouth. No imaging. One attempt reduction in ED unsuccessful due to spasm. Plan: Entonox + IV midazolam, second attempt. If fails, for theatre. Follow-up OMFS clinic re recurrent dislocation.”

Fracture version: “67M fall, hit chin. Mouth open, anterior open bite, can partially close. Tender bilateral preauricular. CT: bilateral condylar fractures. Not TMJ dislocation. For admission, soft diet, OMFS review.”

sections.heading: Do I know the correct reduction manoeuvre? Down then back
items:
If this fails, when will I stop and call for help? 2 attempts max before senior
Safe practice is recognising your limits as well as your skills.

title: Post-operative OMFS Complications
quote: The operation may have finished, but your responsibility has not. The first signs of a complication are often recognised by the junior doctor. Early recognition and escalation prevent small problems becoming major ones.

items:
Why This Module Matters
Most OMFS patients recover uneventfully, but every DCT will review post-op concerns on the ward, in ED, or by phone. The challenge is distinguishing expected recovery — pain, swelling peaking 48–72h, bruising, trismus, minor oozing — from developing complications. You are often first to see the patient. Your assessment, documentation, and timely escalation prevent serious morbidity. Remember: “When reviewing a post-operative patient, always ask yourself: Is this the expected post-operative course, or is something changing?”

sections.heading: Assess the deteriorating post-operative OMFS patient with ABCDE
items: Recognise common complications: haemorrhage, haematoma, infection, dehiscence, airway compromise, nerve deficits

sections.heading: Golden Rule
items: Never reassure yourself because the patient had surgery yesterday. Reassure yourself because you have examined them thoroughly today.

sections.heading: Core Content
items:
BEFORE YOU PHONE YOUR REGISTRAR
Know: □ What operation was performed?, □ When was it performed?, □ Who performed it?, □ What is the specific concern?, □ Current observations?, □ Airway safe?, □ Bleeding?, □ Swelling?, □ Infection?, □ Blood results?, □ Imaging performed?

Initial Assessment – ABCDE
Always begin with ABCDE. Many serious post-op complications present with airway compromise, haemorrhage, sepsis, aspiration, or acute pain. Treat physiological deterioration before focusing on surgical site.

The Expected Post-operative Course
Common and usually normal: mild-moderate pain, facial swelling maximal 48–72h, bruising, limited mouth opening, minor oozing, temporary altered sensation, reduced oral intake. These alone are not complications.

Red Flags 🚨
Immediate senior review if: rapidly increasing swelling, airway compromise, active haemorrhage, difficulty swallowing saliva, fever + systemic deterioration, purulent wound discharge, new cranial nerve deficit, sudden visual disturbance, chest pain/SOB, persistent hypotension or tachycardia.

sections.heading: Common Post-operative Problems
items:
1. Haemorrhage
Ask: Is bleeding active? Has patient swallowed blood? Airway threatened? What procedure?
Management: ABCDE, apply pressure where appropriate, assess haemodynamics, IV access, FBC + clotting + G&S/crossmatch, escalate immediately. Never underestimate concealed bleeding into floor of mouth or neck.

2. Haematoma
Features: progressive swelling, tension, bruising, pain. Large neck haematomas may compromise airway. Urgent senior review. May need return to theatre for evacuation.

3. Surgical Site Infection
Usually develops days after surgery. Look for: increasing pain after initial improvement, erythema, purulent discharge, fever, tenderness, wound breakdown. Management: antibiotics per local guidance, drainage, microbiology sampling, consider imaging if deep collection suspected.

4. Wound Dehiscence
Assess: size, depth, bone/hardware exposure, infection signs. Small mucosal dehiscence may heal conservatively. Larger defects or exposure require senior assessment.

5. Facial Swelling
Expected: gradual ↑ 48–72h, soft, minimal erythema. Concerning: rapid expansion, tense swelling, airway symptoms, severe pain, fever. Consider haematoma, infection, angioedema.

6. Pain Out of Proportion
Severe/worsening pain prompts reassessment. Consider: infection, haematoma, compartment-type pressure, hardware problems, missed diagnosis. Do not just prescribe stronger analgesia without examining.

7. Trismus
Mild common. Worsening trismus may indicate infection, haematoma, deep space collection, TMJ pathology. Measure inter-incisal opening, compare to previous.

8. Nerve Deficits
Document carefully: IAN, lingual, infraorbital, facial nerve. Ask: present immediately post-op? Changed? Complete/partial? New/progressive facial nerve weakness after parotid surgery = urgent consultant review.

9. Hardware Problems
Complaints: mobility, clicking, pain, wound breakdown, plate exposure. Do not manipulate fixation. Image after senior discussion.

10. Airway Compromise
The complication you must never miss. Warning signs: stridor, drooling, voice change, difficulty swallowing, tongue elevation, increasing neck swelling. Call for senior help immediately. Prepare for difficult airway.

Investigations
Targeted to clinical question:
Bloods: FBC, CRP, U&E, clotting, blood cultures if septic.
Imaging: CT with contrast for suspected deep space collection/haematoma, OPG/plain films for hardware, USS for superficial collections.

Assessing the Surgical Site
Ask: Is wound clean? Sutures intact? Discharge? Tissue necrosis? Is swelling expected? Does appearance match symptoms? Compare with operation note if possible.

Reviewing the Operation Note
Before calling consultant, read: indication, findings, difficulties, drains placed, expected post-op instructions. Many questions are answered here.

DCT Checklist: Before You Phone Your Registrar
□ Operation performed + date
□ Current observations + NEWS2
□ Airway status
□ Wound findings
□ Bleeding?
□ Infection?
□ Cranial nerve exam
□ Blood results + imaging
□ What specifically worries you

sections.heading: Read the op note before asking consultant what happened
items: If something “doesn’t look right”, review patient again rather than assume it will settle

sections.heading: Read the operation note — it often explains what you’re seeing
items: Worsening pain, swelling or bleeding deserves reassessment and senior discussion

sections.heading: When in doubt, review again — don’t rely on reassurance alone
items:
Registrar Handover Checklist
Before calling: □ Operation, □ Date of surgery, □ Current obs, □ Airway status, □ Wound findings, □ Bleeding?, □ Infection?, □ CN exam, □ Bloods, □ Imaging, □ What worries you.

Clinical Pearl – The Consultant's Question
If asked: "Why have you called me?"
Avoid: "The patient doesn't look right."
Instead: "This patient is 6h post-ORIF mandible fracture. They’ve developed rapidly increasing submandibular swelling, dysphagia and tachycardia 120 bpm. I'm concerned about expanding haematoma with potential airway compromise and think they need urgent senior review."
Consultants value clear clinical reasoning over certainty.

DCT Survival Box 🚨
The "Five Questions" for Every Post-operative Review
Before leaving bedside:

sections.heading: Have I read the operation note?
items:
If this patient deteriorates overnight, have I documented my assessment and escalation clearly?
Answering these five will identify most significant complications early.

title: OMFS Instruments and Equipment Every DCT Should Know
quote: You do not need to know every instrument on day one—but you should recognise the common ones, understand their purpose and know how to use them safely. Anticipation in theatre begins with knowing the tray.

items:
Why This Module Matters
Every new OMFS DCT remembers standing in theatre hearing “Minnesota,” “Molt,” “Coupland,” “Langenbeck” with no idea what’s wanted. Consultants expect that on day one. Within weeks, you should recognise common instruments, understand their purpose, and anticipate the next step. This module isn’t an exhaustive catalogue — it’s the instruments you’ll use daily in dentoalveolar surgery, trauma, skin surgery, and facial procedures. Remember: Good assistants know the instruments. Great assistants know which one comes next.

sections.heading: Golden Rule
items: Never pass an instrument you cannot identify. If unsure, ask. Nobody expects a new DCT to know every instrument. Everyone expects you to learn.

sections.heading: Trauma instrumentation
items:
1. Examination Instruments
Mouth Mirror: Examination, indirect vision, retraction.
College Tweezers: Handling gauze, small materials, sutures.
Periodontal Probe: Periodontal assessment, measuring defects, pockets.

2. Soft Tissue Instruments
Bard-Parker Scalpel Handle: Usually No.15 blade = workhorse for intraoral/skin incisions, biopsies. No.11 for stab incisions/drains.
Molt No.9 Periosteal Elevator: Most frequently used elevator in OMFS. Raises mucoperiosteal flaps, reflects periosteum, protects tissues. You’ll use this on almost every dentoalveolar list.
Freer Elevator: Delicate tissue elevation. Nasal surgery, septal work, facial trauma.

3. Retractors
Good surgery depends on exposure. Good exposure depends on good retraction.
Minnesota Retractor: Commonest in OMFS. Cheek retraction, flap protection, wisdom teeth. Assistant holds this most of the op.
Langenbeck Retractor: Deeper wounds, facial trauma, neck surgery, skin procedures.
Austin Retractor: Minor oral surgery, facial procedures.
Kilner / Cat’s Paw Retractor: Skin surgery, parotid surgery, delicate soft tissue handling.

4. Elevators
Coupland Elevators: Size 1, 2, 3. Luxating teeth, expanding sockets, root removal.
Warwick James Elevators: Straight, left, right. Excellent for root removal.
Cryer / East-West Elevators: Broken roots, sectioned molars, difficult extractions. Use carefully — high risk of fracture.
Root Picks: Fine instruments for small retained root tips. Avoid excessive force.

5. Extraction Forceps
Initially learn to recognise: Upper incisors, premolars, molars, upper roots. Lower universal, molars, lower roots. Don’t memorise numbers yet — recognition comes with experience.

6. Bone Instruments
Rongeurs / Bone Nibbler: Removing sharp bone, alveoloplasty, bone contouring.
Bone File: Used after rongeurs to smooth sharp bone.
Surgical Curette / Lucas Curette: Granulation tissue, periapical pathology, socket debridement.
Bone Chisel + Mallet: Less common now. Occasional osteotomy, trauma surgery.

7. Suction
Yankauer: Standard suction in OMFS. Rule: suction the blood — not the flap.
Frazier Suction: Fine suction for facial surgery, parotid surgery, delicate dissection.

8. Suturing Instruments
Mayo-Hegar Needle Holder: Standard needle holder. Learn correct grip, needle positioning, hand ties.
Adson Toothed Forceps: Ideal for skin closure — teeth reduce tissue crush.
Non-Toothed Forceps: Delicate tissues, mucosa, dressings.
Suture Scissors: Know where they are. You’ll use constantly.

9. Powered Equipment
Surgical Handpiece: Bone removal, tooth sectioning, osteotomy. Always ensure irrigation working + soft tissues protected.
Straight Handpiece: Wisdom teeth, apicectomy, minor oral surgery.
Sagittal Saw: Trauma, orthognathic. Not commonly handled by DCT but recognise.
Oscillating Saw: Bone grafting, craniofacial, orthognathic.

10. Trauma Instruments
Recognise: drill guides, drill bits, depth gauge, plate benders, screwdrivers, reduction forceps, titanium plates, screws. Initially just understand purpose.

Safe Instrument Passing
Always: pass firmly, present in position it will be used, pass sharps handle first, warn surgeon when passing blade. Never throw instruments onto tray.

Looking After Instruments
Never: drop instruments, use for unintended purposes, damage delicate tips, place heavy instruments on microsurgical ones. Treat with respect — expensive and precision engineered.

Theatre Etiquette
Before every case: introduce yourself to scrub, learn team names, check patient positioning, confirm imaging displayed, wear eye protection. The scrub team teaches you as much as consultants.

DCT Checklist: Before You Assist in Theatre
□ Procedure planned
□ Instruments required
□ Correct handpiece + irrigation available
□ Correct burs
□ Plates/screws if trauma
□ Appropriate sutures
□ Imaging displayed

sections.heading: Best assistants watch the operation — not just the tray
items: A good assistant provides exposure, keeps field clear, anticipates, handles tissues gently, communicates

Registrar Handover Prompt
If asked to prepare: “Procedure is bilateral mandible ORIF. I’ve checked: drill + handpiece + irrigation, 2.0 plates + screws, reduction forceps, Langenbeck retractors, Minnesota, Molt, Yankauer, imaging displayed. Sutures 3-0 Vicryl + 5-0 Prolene ready.”

DCT Survival Box 🚨
Learn These Ten Instruments First
Before month 1 in OMFS, confidently identify:
□ No.3 Bard-Parker scalpel handle
□ Molt No.9 periosteal elevator
□ Minnesota retractor
□ Langenbeck retractor
□ Coupland elevators
□ Warwick James elevators
□ Lucas curette
□ Mayo-Hegar needle holder
□ Adson toothed forceps
□ Yankauer suction
If you recognise these ten without hesitation, you’re ready for most dentoalveolar and minor oral surgery procedures.

Clinical Pearl – The Consultant's Question
If asked: "What makes a good theatre assistant?"
Strong answer: "A good assistant provides excellent exposure, keeps the operative field clear with effective suction, anticipates the next step, handles tissues gently and communicates clearly with the surgeon and scrub team."
Technical knowledge matters, but anticipation, situational awareness and teamwork distinguish an excellent assistant

title: Common Sutures, Needles and Local Anaesthetic in OMFS
quote: Choosing the correct suture or local anaesthetic is not about memorising names—it is about understanding tissue, healing and the procedure you are performing.

items:
Why This Module Matters
As a new OMFS DCT you’ll use LA and sutures daily — clinic, ED, MOS lists, theatre. Consultants don’t expect you to know every product day one. They do expect you to understand principles and use materials safely: which LA to choose, when vasoconstrictors are used/cautioned, suture choice for tissue, needle types, safe injection/suturing, and common pitfalls. Remember: The best closure begins before the first stitch. Gentle tissue handling, good haemostasis and tension-free wound edges matter more than the suture itself.

sections.heading: Golden Rule
items: Always know what you are injecting, how much you have given and why you have chosen it. Never inject a cartridge without checking its contents.

sections.heading: Local Anaesthetic Agents
items:
Vasoconstrictors – Adrenaline
Benefits: ↓bleeding, ↑duration, ↓systemic absorption, improves operative field.
Caution: significant CVD, uncontrolled arrhythmias, unstable angina, MI <6 months, phaeochromocytoma, severe hyperthyroidism. Use clinical judgement + local guidance.

Maximum Recommended Doses – Calculate Every Time
Depends on: agent, patient weight, age/frailty, hepatic function, comorbidities. Never rely on cartridge number alone. If unsure, calculate or ask.
Key examples — always check BNF/local protocol:
Lidocaine + adrenaline: 7 mg/kg. 2.2ml cartridge = 44mg → 70kg adult max ∼11 cartridges.
Articaine + adrenaline: 7 mg/kg. 1.7ml cartridge = 68mg → 70kg adult max ∼7 cartridges.
Mepivacaine plain: 4.4 mg/kg → 70kg adult max ∼6 cartridges.

Bupivacaine: 2 mg/kg.
In children/elderly reduce. Max doses lower in liver disease.

Before You Inject – Checklist
□ Correct patient, □ Correct procedure, □ Allergies, □ Medical history, □ Anticoagulants, □ LA selected + expiry checked, □ Aspiration before injection, □ Total dose documented.

Injection Principles
Explain, position patient, dry mucosa, topical if appropriate, stretch tissues, inject slowly, aspirate before injecting, observe afterwards. Slow injections = less painful + ↓ intravascular risk.

Common LA Techniques
Become familiar with: buccal infiltration, palatal infiltration, IANB, long buccal, mental, infraorbital, greater palatine, nasopalatine blocks. Understand anatomy before independent practice.

Local Anaesthetic Toxicity – Recognise It
Rare but emergency. Early: circumoral numbness, metallic taste, tinnitus, dizziness, agitation, slurred speech. Severe: seizures, ↓GCS, arrhythmias, arrest. Stop injecting, call for help, follow local LAST protocol — Intralipid 20%.

sections.heading: Common Suture Materials
items:
Suture Sizes
Common OMFS: 3-0, 4-0, 5-0, 6-0. Rule: face deserves finer sutures than scalp. More zeros = finer. 6-0 finer than 3-0.

Needle Types
Reverse Cutting: Commonest in OMFS. Excellent for skin, strong, ↓tissue tearing.
Cutting: Tough tissues, oral mucosa.
Taper / Round-bodied: Delicate soft tissues, muscle. Less used for skin.

Basic Suturing Principles
Aim: gentle tissue handling, accurate wound edge approximation, minimal tension, good haemostasis, even spacing. Suture should approximate — not strangulate — tissue.

Common Techniques
Confident with: simple interrupted, horizontal mattress, vertical mattress, figure-of-eight, continuous, subcuticular. Simple interrupted = foundation.

Instrument Handling
Needle holder dominant hand, tissue forceps non-dominant. Never grasp needle with forceps if avoidable. Hold needle 2/3 from tip.
Knot Tying: Master instrument ties, two-handed, one-handed. Secure knot > elegant knot.

DCT Checklist: If Preparing for Dentoalveolar Procedure
□ LA: Lidocaine 2% + adrenaline unless contraindicated
□ Needle: short/long dental depending on block
□ Suture: 3-0 or 4-0 Vicryl Rapide® for intraoral
□ Instruments: needle holder, Adson forceps, suture scissors

sections.heading: Wound healing depends on technique more than suture brand
items:
Registrar Handover Checklist
If discussing wound closure: □ Mechanism, □ Tissue involved, □ Contamination, □ Nerve/duct injury?, □ Closure performed, □ Suture material + size, □ Antibiotics?, □ Follow-up arranged.

Clinical Pearl – The Consultant's Question
If asked: "What is the most important principle of wound closure?"
Strong answer: "Achieving accurate, tension-free tissue approximation while preserving tissue blood supply. The suture should support healing, not compensate for poor surgical technique."
Quality of closure is determined before the final knot.

DCT Survival Box 🚨
The Everyday OMFS Set-Up
For routine dentoalveolar procedure think:
LA: Lidocaine 2% + adrenaline unless contraindicated
Needle: Short or long dental depending on injection
Suture: 3-0 or 4-0 Vicryl Rapide® intraoral
Instruments: Needle holder, Adson forceps, suture scissors
Knowing this standard set-up prepares you for most routine oral surgery and helps anticipate consultant needs.

Common Mistakes ⚠️
Forgetting to calculate max dose, injecting too quickly, failing to aspirate, crushing tissues, overtightening sutures, wound tension, unnecessarily large sutures for facial skin.

title: Interpreting Common OMFS Radiographs
quote: Never look at an X-ray simply to confirm what you think you know. Look at it systematically, because the most important finding is often the one you were not expecting.

items:
Why This Module Matters
Radiographs are integral to OMFS. As a DCT you’ll review imaging in ED, clinic, ward rounds and theatre. The skill is systematic interpretation — not spot diagnosis. Radiographs complement, but never replace, history and examination. This module covers common OMFS modalities and gives you a structured approach so you don’t miss the second mandibular fracture, the antral carcinoma, or the IAC running through a molar root.

sections.heading: Golden Rule
items: Every radiograph deserves a systematic review—even if the diagnosis seems obvious. Never look only at the area of interest. Always review the entire image.

sections.heading: Core Content
items:
BEFORE YOU REVIEW ANY RADIOGRAPH
Ask: □ Is this the correct patient?, □ Is the image correctly labelled?, □ What imaging modality is this?, □ Why was the image taken?, □ What clinical question am I trying to answer?

Common Imaging Modalities in OMFS
Become familiar with: Periapical PA, Bitewing, DPT/OPT, Occlusal, CBCT, CT facial bones, CT neck with contrast, Ultrasound, MRI.

sections.heading: A Systematic Approach – Every Time
items:
Step 1 – Confirm Patient Details
Name, DOB, NHS/hospital number, date of imaging. Wrong patient = wrong treatment.

Step 2 – Image Quality
Is it diagnostic? Movement? Anatomy adequately visualised? Repeat required? Poor films mislead.

Step 3 – Review the Entire Image
Never zoom into pathology first. Look at: bones, teeth, sinuses, soft tissues where visible, airway, TMJs, cervical spine if included. Many incidental findings discovered this way.

Dental Panoramic Tomography (OPT/DPT)
The commonest OMFS image. Assess systematically:

Teeth: Missing, impacted, caries, root morphology, periapical pathology, retained roots.
Bone: Cortical continuity, fractures, bone loss, cysts, tumours, osteomyelitis.
Inferior Alveolar Canal: Always identify position, corticated borders, relationship to lower 8s. Look for: interruption of superior border, darkening of roots, diversion, narrowing. Critical before lower third molar surgery.
Maxillary Sinuses: Opacification, fluid levels, mucosal thickening, foreign bodies, bony destruction.
TMJs: Condylar shape, cortical outline, symmetry, degenerative change.

Periapical Radiographs
Ideal for: individual teeth, root morphology, PDL space, periapical lesions, endodontics. Look at: lamina dura, root apex, furcation, crestal bone.

Bitewing Radiographs
Best for: proximal caries, crestal bone levels, existing restorations. Do NOT use to diagnose apical pathology.

Occlusal Radiographs
Useful for: salivary stones, impacted teeth, foreign bodies, floor of mouth pathology, cortical expansion.

Cone Beam CT (CBCT)
High-resolution 3D of dentoalveolar skeleton. Indications: impacted teeth, roots vs IAN, implant planning, jaw pathology, endodontics, selected trauma. Excellent for bone, limited soft tissue. Review entire volume, not just region of interest.

CT Facial Bones
Investigation of choice for most facial fractures. Assess systematically: mandible, maxilla, zygomas, orbits, nasal bones, frontal sinus, skull base. Review axial, coronal, sagittal. 3D recons for visualisation only — never replace axial/coronal/sagittal review.

CT Neck with Contrast
For: deep neck space infection, salivary abscess, neck collections, airway compromise, malignancy. Look for: rim-enhancing collections, gas, fascial plane involvement, airway deviation/narrowing, vascular complications.

Ultrasound
Indications: salivary gland disease, neck lumps, abscesses, lymph nodes. Advantages: no radiation, dynamic, guided aspiration.

MRI
Best for: soft tissue tumours, salivary lesions, TMJ disc, perineural spread, osteomyelitis. Superior soft tissue contrast vs CT.

sections.heading: Common Radiographic Findings
items:
Incidental Findings
Never ignore: impacted teeth, carotid calcification, retained roots, bone lesions, elongated styloid, cervical spine degeneration. Document significant findings and discuss appropriately.

Red Flags 🚨
Escalate immediately: displaced mandible fractures, midface instability, orbital floor defect with entrapment, airway narrowing on CT neck, rim-enhancing collection with gas, IAC running through molar roots with signs of compression, unexpected malignancy features: bony destruction, periosteal reaction.

Presenting Radiographic Findings
Structured example: “This is a panoramic radiograph of the correct patient taken today. There is a mesioangular impacted LL8 with intimate radiographic relationship to the IAC demonstrated by interruption of the superior cortical border and darkening of the roots. No associated cystic change seen. Remaining dentition and jaws show no other significant abnormality.”

DCT Checklist: Before Discussing Imaging with Registrar
□ Imaging modality + date
□ Main abnormality + side
□ Relationship to important structures — IAC, maxillary sinus, orbital floor
□ Evidence of infection? Fracture?
□ Soft tissue involvement?
□ Incidental findings?
□ Your interpretation

sections.heading: When uncertain, ask for senior review rather than guessing
items:
Clinical Pearl – The Consultant's Question
If asked: "What is the commonest mistake junior doctors make when interpreting radiographs?"
Good answer: "They search for the expected abnormality instead of reviewing the entire image systematically. This leads to satisfaction-of-search error, where identifying one lesion causes additional important findings to be overlooked."
Developing a consistent search pattern is one of the most valuable habits in OMFS.

DCT Survival Box 🚨
The "IMAGE" Rule
Whenever you review an OMFS radiograph, remember IMAGE:
I – Identity: Is this the correct patient?
M – Modality: What type of imaging is this?
A – Anatomy: Review the entire image systematically.
G – Generate a differential: Correlate radiographic findings with clinical picture.
E – Escalate if uncertain: Never be afraid to seek senior advice.

Common Mistakes ⚠️
Looking only at tooth of interest, missing second mandibular fracture, ignoring maxillary sinuses on OPT, overcalling normal anatomy as pathology, forgetting to identify IAC before lower 8s, failing to review whole CBCT volume.

title: The First 100 Days – Becoming a Safe and Confident OMFS DCT
quote: Competence in OMFS is not achieved in a week or a month. It develops through curiosity, reflection, repetition and the humility to ask for help. Your goal is not to know everything—it is to become a doctor your patients and colleagues can trust.

items:
Why This Module Matters
Technical skills get you through procedures. Non-technical skills get you through the job. The first 100 days of OMFS are steep, disorienting, and exhausting. You’ll feel slow, uncertain, and hyper-aware of what you don’t know. That’s normal. This module is about surviving and thriving: how to build trust, recognise your limits, learn from each case, and become the DCT that nurses bleep first because you’re safe. Patients remember how you made them feel. Consultants remember whether you were reliable. Your aim isn’t perfection — it’s progression.

sections.heading: Golden Rule
items: Be safe before you are fast. Be kind before you are clever. Be honest before you are right.

sections.heading: The Non-Negotiables – Do These Every Day
items: Show up 10min early. Check your bleeps, review the list, look at inpatients before handover.
Read the operation note on every post-op patient you review. Most questions are answered there.
Write your name + bleep + time on every entry. Own your decisions.
Reassess after every intervention. If you gave fluids, recheck BP. If you reduced a jaw, recheck occlusion.
Debrief yourself. After every shift ask: What went well? What would I do differently? What do I need to learn?

sections.heading:
Competence ≠ Knowing Everything
Competence =
items: Recognising sick vs not sick within 30 seconds.
Starting ABCDE without being told.
Knowing your hard limits and calling before you cross them.
Communicating so others aren’t surprised by your patient’s condition at 3am.

Escalation: The Skill That Saves Careers
Call early if: NEWS2 ↑, airway concern, active bleeding, you’ve done 2 interventions with no improvement, you’re thinking “should I call?” — that’s your answer.
How to call: Use SBAR. Be specific about what you need: “I need you to come and see” vs “FYI”. Never apologise for calling. Apologise if you don’t call and harm occurs.

sections.heading: Building Trust – The Currency of OMFS
items:
With Nurses: Answer bleeps. Say thank you. If they’re worried, you’re worried. Close the loop: “Thanks for calling, I’ve reviewed, plan is X”.
With ED: See referrals promptly. Give a decision. Don’t sit on patients. Write clear plans.
With Registrars: Be prepared before you call. Know obs, PMH, what you’ve done. Take feedback without ego.
With Consultants: Be honest. Be prepared for theatre. Know your patients. Follow up tasks.
With Patients: Introduce yourself. Explain in plain English. Admit when you don’t know. They forgive ignorance, not arrogance.

sections.heading:
Reflection – Your Superpower
After a difficult case, ask:
items: What happened? Facts only.

sections.heading: So what? Why did it matter? What did I feel?
items:
Now what? What will I change next time?
Write it down. One paragraph per week. You’ll be shocked how fast you improve.

sections.heading: Looking After Yourself
items: Sleep: Protect post-nights. No one is safe on 2h sleep.
Food: Carry snacks. Hypoglycaemia makes you irritable and stupid.
Support: Find your people — other DCTs, regs, mentors. Talk.
Boundaries: You can’t fix the whole hospital. Do your best, handover, go home.
Mistakes: You will make them. Disclose, reflect, learn. That’s how consultants were made.

DCT Checklist: Weekly Review
□ One new clinical skill learned?
□ One piece of feedback requested + acted on?
□ One patient I’m proud of how I managed?
□ One system issue I flagged to improve care?
□ Did I eat, sleep, exercise at least 3x this week?

sections.heading: Be the DCT you’d want looking after your family — that’s the standard

title: Medical Emergencies in OMFS
quote: Medical emergencies are uncommon, but when they occur there is no time to open a textbook. Preparation, teamwork and a structured approach save lives.

items:
Why This Module Matters
OMFS patients can have medical emergencies unrelated to surgery: vasovagal syncope in clinic, anaphylaxis to LA/antibiotics, seizures, hypoglycaemia, MI, cardiac arrest. You may be first on scene in clinic, ward, or theatre. There is no time to revise — preparation + ABCDE + teamwork saves lives. Your role: recognise, initiate immediate management, call for help early, and communicate clearly. The sickest patient is not always surgical.

sections.heading: Apply ABCDE approach to any collapsed/unwell OMFS patient
items: Recognise and initiate management of common emergencies: syncope, anaphylaxis, seizure, hypoglycaemia, chest pain, cardiac arrest, LAST

sections.heading: Golden Rule
items: Treat what you find. If airway/breathing/circulation is compromised, act now and get help — don’t wait for a diagnosis.

sections.heading: Core Content
items:
BEFORE YOU FACE ANY EMERGENCY
Know: □ Where is O2 + BVM?, □ Where is crash trolley/AED?, □ How to call 2222/MET call?, □ Who is your anaesthetic/senior help?, □ Where is emergency drugs box?, □ What is baseline for this patient?

Universal Approach – ABCDE + DRSABCD
Danger – ensure scene safe
Response – AVPU. If unresponsive → shout for help + 2222
Send for help – call crash team early
Airway – open with head tilt/chin lift or jaw thrust if C-spine concern. Suction. Consider adjuncts
Breathing – look/listen/feel. RR, SpO2, work of breathing. O2 15L non-rebreather if hypoxic. BVM if not breathing adequately
Circulation – pulse, BP, CRT, bleeding. IV access. Fluid challenge if hypotensive.
Disability – GCS, pupils, BM. Treat hypoglycaemia
Exposure – temp, rashes, swelling. Don’t miss anaphylaxis

sections.heading: Common OMFS Medical Emergencies
items:
1. Vasovagal Syncope / Faint
Trigger: Pain, sight of blood, LA injection, anxiety.
Signs: Pallor, sweating, nausea, bradycardia, hypotension, transient LOC.
Management: Lie flat, legs elevated. O2 if needed. Recovery in seconds–minutes. Check BM, HR, BP. Don’t sit up too quickly. Reassure. If LOC prolonged >1min or not recovering → treat as collapse, call help.

2. Anaphylaxis
Trigger: Antibiotics, LA, latex, chlorhexidine.
Signs: ABC problem. Rapid onset. Airway: swelling, hoarseness. Breathing: wheeze, stridor. Circulation: hypotension, tachycardia. Skin: urticaria, flushing.
Management – Resus Council UK:
Call for help. 2222.
Remove trigger. Lie flat, legs up unless breathing difficulty.
Adrenaline IM 0.5mg 1:1000 anterolateral thigh. Repeat 5min if no improvement.
O2 15L, IV access, fluid bolus 500–1000ml.

Chlorphenamine 10mg + Hydrocortisone 200mg IV/IM.
If airway threatened → anaesthetics + prepare for difficult airway. Biphasic reactions can occur — observe 6–12h.

3. Local Anaesthetic Systemic Toxicity LAST
Trigger: Inadvertent IV injection, excessive dose.
Early: Perioral tingling, metallic taste, tinnitus, agitation, slurred speech.
Late: Seizures, ↓GCS, arrhythmias, CV collapse.
Management: Stop injecting. Call for help + anaesthetics. ABCDE. Intralipid 20%: 1.5ml/kg bolus over 1min, then infusion 15ml/kg/hr. CPR if arrest — prolonged efforts may be needed. AAGBI LAST guideline.

4. Seizure
Common: Epilepsy, alcohol withdrawal, hypoglycaemia, hypoxia.
Management: Safe environment, time seizure, O2, BM. Do not restrain. Recovery position post-ictal. If >5min or repeated → status: benzodiazepine per local protocol: buccal midazolam 10mg or IV lorazepam 4mg. Call anaesthetics. Check glucose, U&E, calcium.

5. Hypoglycaemia
Risk: Diabetics, fasting pre-op, alcoholics.
Signs: Sweating, agitation, confusion, seizures, coma. BM <4.0 mmol/L.
Management: If conscious: 15–20g fast-acting glucose orally. If unconscious: IV 10% glucose 150–200ml or IM glucagon 1mg. Recheck BM 10min. Find cause.

6. Chest Pain / ACS
Consider: MI, angina, PE, aortic dissection.
Signs: Crushing chest pain, radiation to arm/jaw, SOB, nausea, sweating.
Management: Call for help. Sit up. O2 if hypoxic. GTN spray if BP OK. Aspirin 300mg chewed. ECG + troponin. If STEMI → cath lab. If arrest → ALS.

sections.heading:
7. Cardiac Arrest
Management – ALS:
items: Confirm unresponsive + not breathing normally. Call 2222 + start CPR.
30 compressions : 2 breaths, rate 100–120/min, depth 5–6cm.
Attach defibrillator — shock if VF/VT.
Adrenaline 1mg IV every 3–5min. Amiodarone 300mg after 3rd shock.
Reversible causes: 4Hs + 4Ts. Hypoxia, hypovolaemia, hypo/hyperkalaemia, hypothermia, tamponade, tension pneumothorax, toxins, thrombosis.

Emergency Drugs – Know Location
Adrenaline 1:1000 IM, Atropine, Glucagon, Glucose 10%, Hydrocortisone, Chlorphenamine, Midazolam, Aspirin, GTN, Salbutamol neb, Intralipid 20%. Know your crash trolley.

Red Flags 🚨
Call for senior help immediately if: unresponsive, airway noise, RR <8 or >30, SpO2 <90% on O2, HR <40 or >130, SBP <90, GCS drop ≥2, seizure >5min, chest pain, suspected anaphylaxis, any LAST signs.

DCT Checklist: In a Medical Emergency
□ Safe approach + call for help
□ ABCDE assessment started
□ O2 on + monitoring
□ IV access
□ BM checked
□ Emergency drugs given per protocol
□ SBAR handover ready
□ Document timed events

sections.heading: Final Message to the Reader
items: Congratulations.
By completing this handbook, you have acquired the foundations required to become a safe and effective OMFS Dental Core Trainee.
You will continue learning every day throughout your career.

The best OMFS clinicians are not those who know every answer—they are those who remain curious, seek help when needed, treat every patient with compassion and strive to improve with every clinical encounter.
We hope this handbook accompanies you through your first year in OMFS and remains a trusted reference whenever you need it.
Welcome to the specialty.
Good luck.

title: Post-Operative Head & Neck Cancer Surgery
quote: You are not expected to know everything. You are expected to recognise when something is wrong and get the right person involved early.

items: Post-operative head and neck cancer patients are among the most complex patients you will encounter on an OMFS/maxillofacial ward.

Major oral cavity or oropharyngeal resection
Composite resection and neck dissection
Free-flap reconstruction
Pedicled flap reconstruction
Tracheostomy
Total laryngectomy
Pharyngectomy
Mandibulectomy/maxillectomy
Skin resection and reconstruction
PEG insertion
Multiple drains
Complex vascular anastomoses
The patient can therefore deteriorate rapidly from airway compromise, haemorrhage, flap compromise, sepsis, aspiration, electrolyte disturbance, chyle leak or nutritional problems.

For the DCT, the key principle is:
"You do not need to manage these patients alone. You do need to recognise deterioration early, start appropriate immediate management and escalate promptly."

sections.heading: Learning Objectives
items:
Identify the major components of a head and neck cancer operation.
Perform a structured post-operative assessment.
Recognise potentially life-threatening airway problems.
Understand the difference between a tracheostomy and a laryngectomy.
Perform and interpret basic free-flap observations.
Recognise early signs of flap compromise.
Identify post-operative neck haematoma and haemorrhage.
Recognise chyle leak.
Recognise salivary/pharyngeal fistula.
Assess wounds, drains and reconstruction.
Understand the principles of post-operative nutrition and fluid management.
Recognise sepsis, respiratory deterioration and thromboembolic disease.
Know when to contact the registrar, consultant, anaesthetics, ENT, ICU/HDU or other specialist teams.
Document an appropriate post-operative assessment and escalation plan.

sections.heading: Golden Rule: Know the Operation
items:
Before examining the patient, find out:
"What exactly did they have done?"
Do not start by assuming that every head and neck cancer patient has simply had "a neck dissection and flap". Read the operation note.
Identify the following:

Resection
Primary tumour site
Structures removed
Mandibulectomy/maxillectomy
Tongue resection
Floor-of-mouth resection
Pharyngeal resection
Skin resection
Parotid/submandibular gland surgery

Neck
Side of neck dissection
Levels dissected
Structures sacrificed
Carotid involvement
Internal jugular vein sacrifice
Spinal accessory nerve sacrifice/preservation
Hypoglossal nerve
Vagus nerve
Phrenic nerve
Thoracic duct region

Reconstruction
Free flap
Pedicled flap
Local flap
Skin graft
Primary closure

If free flap:
Flap type
Artery
Vein
Anastomosis
Recipient vessels
Implantable Doppler if used
Monitoring protocol

Airway
Tracheostomy?
Laryngectomy?
Tube type and size?
Cuffed/uncuffed?
Fenestrated?
Sutured or secured?
Any airway concerns?

Feeding
NG tube?
PEG/RIG?

Drains

sections.heading: The First Five Minutes at the Bedside
items: If called because the patient is unwell:

The key question:
"What has changed from this patient's previous baseline?"

The A–E Quick Check
A – AIRWAY — Is the patient talking? Is there stridor? Is there airway obstruction? Is the tracheostomy patent? Is the tube displaced? Is there blood/secretions obstructing the tube? Is this a laryngectomy patient?
B – BREATHING — Respiratory rate; oxygen saturations; work of breathing; chest movement; breath sounds; oxygen requirement.
C – CIRCULATION — Heart rate; blood pressure; capillary refill; peripheral perfusion; bleeding; drain output; neck swelling; urine output.
D – DISABILITY — Conscious level; confusion; pain; blood glucose if appropriate.
E – EXPOSURE — Neck; flap; wound; drains; donor site; tracheostomy; chest; abdomen; legs for DVT signs.

sections.heading: The Post-Operative Head & Neck Cancer Ward Round
items: A useful sequence is:
Airway → Flap → Neck → Wound → Drains → Nutrition → Fluids/electrolytes → Respiratory status → Pain → Mobility/VTE → Blood results → Antibiotics/medications → Rehabilitation → Discharge planning

sections.heading: Airway – Your First Priority
items: Head and neck cancer surgery can completely alter normal airway anatomy.

Oedema
Bleeding
Haematoma
Secretions
Mucus plugging
Tube obstruction
Tube displacement
False passage
Aspiration
Flap swelling
Pharyngeal swelling
Infection
Pneumonia
Never assume the airway is secure because the patient has a tracheostomy.
A tracheostomy can become blocked, displaced, decannulated, malpositioned, or obstructed by secretions or blood.

sections.heading: Tracheostomy vs Laryngectomy
items: This distinction is critical.
Tracheostomy

The patient usually retains a connection between the upper airway and lungs. Therefore, depending on the circumstances, oxygenation may potentially be achieved through the face, mouth/nose or tracheostomy.
Total laryngectomy
The patient's airway is permanently separated from the mouth and nose.
A laryngectomy patient breathes exclusively through the neck stoma.
DCT Survival Box
If you encounter a patient with a neck stoma in an emergency: "Find out immediately whether this is a tracheostomy or a laryngectomy." If uncertain, seek urgent senior/airway assistance.

sections.heading: Tracheostomy Emergency
items:
If a tracheostomy patient deteriorates:
Call for help.
Assess ABC.
Give oxygen.
Assess the patient, not just the monitor.
Remove obvious obstruction if appropriate.
Check tube position and patency.
Suction if indicated.
Follow the patient's tracheostomy emergency algorithm/local protocol.
Involve anaesthetics/ENT/OMFS/critical care early where appropriate.

Red flags
Sudden desaturation
Increasing respiratory effort
No airflow through tube
Unable to pass suction catheter
High airway resistance
New bleeding
Tube displacement
Subcutaneous emphysema
Rapid neck swelling
A blocked or displaced tracheostomy is an airway emergency.
Follow your local tracheostomy emergency algorithm and obtain expert airway assistance early.

sections.heading: Free-Flap Monitoring
items: Free-flap reconstruction is one of the most important reasons these patients require close post-operative observation.
The flap depends on arterial inflow, venous drainage and patent microvascular anastomoses. Failure can result in flap loss.

Depending on the flap and local protocol, assess:
Colour
Temperature
Turgor
Capillary refill
Pin-prick bleeding where prescribed
Doppler signal
Swelling
Congestion
Comparison with previous observations

The most important principle:
"Know what the flap looked and sounded like previously."
A single observation is less useful than a change from baseline.

sections.heading: Flap Red Flags
items: What should the DCT do?

Escalate immediately. Do not wait until the next ward round. Do not assume that a flap with a marginal observation will "probably improve". Do not repeatedly manipulate the flap yourself while waiting for senior review.

DCT Survival Rule
"A potentially compromised free flap is a time-critical surgical problem."

sections.heading: Neck Dissection
items:
After neck dissection, inspect for:
Haematoma
Seroma
Wound breakdown
Infection
Salivary leak
Chyle leak
Skin flap necrosis
Facial/neck swelling
Neurological deficit
Know whether major structures were preserved or sacrificed.

Possible post-operative neurological findings include shoulder weakness, tongue weakness, lower facial weakness, vocal cord dysfunction and sensory changes. The significance depends on the operative findings and structures involved.

sections.heading: Post-Operative Neck Haematoma
items: This is one of the most important complications to recognise.

Clinical features
Increasing neck swelling
Tight neck
Pain
Bruising
Increasing drain output or surprisingly little drain output
Dysphagia
Respiratory difficulty
Stridor
Venous congestion
Anxiety/restlessness
Tachycardia
Hypotension
Critical point:
A drain does not exclude a neck haematoma.
A drain may be blocked, kinked, displaced, too small to drain the collection, or positioned away from the bleeding point.

Management
Call senior surgical help immediately.
ABC assessment.
Oxygen.
IV access.
Bloods/crossmatch as appropriate.
Activate local major haemorrhage pathway if indicated.
Early anaesthetic/critical care involvement.
Prepare for urgent return to theatre if required.

DCT Survival Box
"Neck swelling + airway symptoms after major head and neck surgery = emergency until proven otherwise."

sections.heading: Drains
items: Never write: "Drains fine."

Instead document:
Number of drains
Location
Amount
Character
Trend
Suction status
Whether functioning

sections.heading: Chyle Leak
items: The thoracic duct and right lymphatic duct can be injured during neck dissection.

A chyle leak may present as:
Increasing drain output
Milky/creamy drainage
Increased output after feeding
Neck swelling
Fluid collection
Electrolyte disturbance
Protein loss
Nutritional depletion
Immunological compromise

Think about chyle leak when:
"Drain output becomes milky, particularly after enteral feeding."
Management depends on volume of leak, timing, patient condition, surgical anatomy and local protocol.
Treatment may involve dietary modification, specialist dietetic input, drain management, pharmacological treatment in selected cases, or surgical intervention for persistent/high-output leaks.
Do not independently change enteral feeding without discussing the plan with the surgical and dietetic teams.

sections.heading: Salivary Leak / Pharyngeal Fistula
items: Following oral/pharyngeal cancer surgery, leakage may occur from the oral cavity, pharynx, anastomosis or salivary gland region.

Look for:
Increasing drain output
Cloudy/salivary drainage
Wound wetness
Foul smell
Skin maceration
Neck swelling
Fever
Wound breakdown
A fistula can subsequently lead to infection, abscess, carotid exposure and wound breakdown.
DCT action
Escalate early. Do not simply document "possible saliva leak" and wait several days.

sections.heading: Wound Infection and Dehiscence
items:
Assess:
Erythema
Swelling
Warmth
Tenderness
Discharge
Purulence
Wound separation
Skin necrosis
Flap viability
Odour

Check systemic features:
Fever
Tachycardia
Hypotension
Confusion
Rising inflammatory markers
Increasing oxygen requirement
A normal temperature does not exclude infection or sepsis.

sections.heading: Nutrition, Hydration and Swallowing
items: Major head and neck cancer surgery can significantly impair oral intake, swallowing, speech, taste, saliva and mastication.

Patients may require:
NG feeding
PEG feeding
RIG feeding
Modified diets
Thickened fluids
Speech and language therapy
Dietetic support

The DCT should know:
Is the patient NBM?
Why?
What is the feeding route?
What is the current feeding regimen?
Is the patient tolerating feeds?
Is there a dietetic plan?
Has SLT reviewed the patient?
Are medications being administered appropriately?
Is there an adequate fluid prescription?

Avoid the common mistake:
"Not eating" ≠ "nothing to worry about because they have a PEG."
Patients can still become dehydrated, malnourished, electrolyte depleted, hyperglycaemic, constipated or overloaded.

sections.heading: Refeeding Risk
items: Patients with prolonged poor intake may be at risk of refeeding syndrome.

Think about:
Phosphate
Potassium
Magnesium
Thiamine
Fluid balance
High-risk patients require appropriate nutritional assessment and monitoring according to local/NICE protocols.

DCT Survival Box
"Starting feeds is not simply a matter of prescribing calories. Know the patient's nutritional risk and follow the dietetic/medical plan."

sections.heading: VTE and Anticoagulation
items: These patients can have significant thromboembolic risk because of major cancer surgery, malignancy, reduced mobility, age/comorbidity and prolonged hospitalisation.

Check:
VTE assessment
Mechanical prophylaxis
Pharmacological prophylaxis
Renal function
Bleeding risk
Timing around surgery/procedures
But remember: head and neck cancer surgery also carries a significant bleeding risk.
Do not independently start, stop or alter anticoagulation without understanding the surgical plan and discussing it with the appropriate senior team.

sections.heading: Fluids and Electrolytes
items: These patients can become "quietly unwell".

Monitor:
Sodium
Potassium
Magnesium
Phosphate
Calcium
Urea
Creatinine
Glucose
Haemoglobin

Also assess:
Fluid balance
Urine output
Drain losses
Enteral losses
IV fluid administration
Particular attention: high-output drains can produce significant fluid and electrolyte losses.
Do not simply look at the blood results in isolation.

Ask:
"What has the patient lost, and what have we replaced?"

sections.heading: Respiratory Complications
items:
Atelectasis
Mucus plugging
Aspiration
Pneumonia
Pulmonary oedema
COPD exacerbation
Hypoventilation
Pulmonary embolism

Assess:
Respiratory rate
Oxygen requirement
Work of breathing
Chest examination
Cough
Secretions
Ability to clear secretions
Chest X-ray if indicated
A patient whose oxygen requirement is steadily increasing needs assessment. Do not simply keep increasing oxygen without identifying why.

sections.heading: Pain
items: Good analgesia is important because poorly controlled pain can impair breathing, coughing, mobilisation, sleep and nutrition.

Review:
Pain score
Site
Character
Analgesic requirements
Paracetamol
Opioids
NSAIDs where appropriate
Neuropathic pain agents where prescribed

Watch for opioid complications:
Sedation
Respiratory depression
Nausea
Constipation
Delirium

sections.heading: Delirium and Confusion
items: A new change in behaviour or cognition should not simply be labelled "confused post-op".

Look for reversible causes:
Infection
Hypoxia
Hypercapnia
Pain
Urinary retention
Constipation
Electrolyte disturbance
Dehydration
Medication effects
Sleep deprivation
Escalate significant or unexplained deterioration.

sections.heading: Communication, Speech and Psychological Care
items: Head and neck cancer surgery can profoundly affect speech, swallowing, appearance, facial movement, social interaction, body image, independence, employment and psychological wellbeing.

Patients may require input from:
SLT
Dietitians
Specialist nurses
Physiotherapists
Occupational therapists
Psychology
Prosthodontics
Restorative dentistry
Community services

DCT principle
"Do not focus exclusively on the surgical wound. The patient is more than the flap."

sections.heading: What Is the DCT's Job?
items:
Recognise → Assess → Act → Escalate → Document → Reassess
Recognise: Identify abnormal findings.
Assess: Perform an appropriate clinical assessment.
Act: Start immediate appropriate management.
Escalate: Tell the registrar/consultant early.
Document: Record what you found, what you did and who you contacted.
Reassess: Do not assume that because someone has reviewed the patient, your responsibility to monitor them has ended.

sections.heading: When to Call the Senior Immediately
items:
Consultant-level principle
"If you are worried enough to think 'I wonder if I should call the registrar', call the registrar."

sections.heading: The Post-Operative Handover
items:
A good handover should include:
"This is a [age]-year-old patient, day X following [operation]."

Then:
Airway – tracheostomy/laryngectomy, tube details, current oxygen requirement.
Flap – type, viability, Doppler, any concerns.
Neck – wound, swelling, drain output.
Nutrition – oral/NG/PEG, feeding regimen, SLT/dietetic plan.
Bloods – Hb, WCC/CRP, renal function, electrolytes.
Current issues – infection, chyle, fistula, respiratory issue, pain, mobility.
Plan – what needs doing today, what needs monitoring and what requires escalation.

sections.heading: Documentation
items: A useful post-operative entry should allow another clinician to understand the patient's current status.

sections.heading: Discharge Planning Starts Early
items: Discharge is not simply: "Wound looks good — home."

Consider:
Airway – Is the patient decannulated? Is stoma care understood? Is equipment available?
Nutrition – Oral intake? NG? PEG? Feeding plan? Community dietetic support?
Wound – Dressings? Drain? Suture/staple plan?
Medication – Analgesia, antibiotics, anticoagulation and other regular medication.
Rehabilitation – SLT, dietetics, physiotherapy, OT and community support.
Follow-up – Surgical team, oncology, MDT, SLT, dietetics, restorative/prosthodontic services as required.

sections.heading: Consultant Pearls
items:
Pearl 1
"Know the operation before you interpret the observations."

Pearl 2
"A tracheostomy is not the same as a laryngectomy."

Pearl 3
"A changing flap is more important than a single flap observation."

Pearl 4
"Neck swelling after major neck surgery is an emergency until proven otherwise."

Pearl 5
"A functioning drain does not exclude a haematoma."

Pearl 6
"Milky drain fluid should make you think of chyle."

Pearl 7
"Salivary-looking drainage from a neck wound is not "just another drain"."

Pearl 8
"Do not wait for blood results before recognising a sick patient."

Pearl 9
"The patient's clinical trajectory matters more than an isolated number."

Pearl 10
"If the patient is deteriorating, escalate while you investigate — not after you have finished investigating."

sections.heading: The Golden DCT Rule
items: When reviewing a complex post-operative head and neck cancer patient:
AIRWAY → FLAP → BLEEDING → SEPSIS → NUTRITION → FLUIDS → DRAINS → WOUND → RESPIRATORY STATUS → REHABILITATION

And remember:
"You are not expected to know everything. You are expected to recognise when something is wrong and get the right person involved early."

sections.heading: Key Take-Home Message
items: Major head and neck cancer surgery produces patients with multiple simultaneous potential points of failure.
The DCT's role is not to become the reconstructive surgeon, intensivist, airway specialist, dietitian and oncologist overnight.
Your role is to:
Recognise → Assess → Stabilise → Escalate → Document → Reassess
The most dangerous mistakes are often not failures of advanced surgical knowledge. They are:

Not recognising an airway problem
Not recognising a neck haematoma
Missing a compromised flap
Ignoring a change in drain output
Failing to recognise sepsis
Assuming a patient is well because their observations are initially normal
Failing to escalate early
SEE THE PATIENT. KNOW THE OPERATION. RECOGNISE THE CHANGE. CALL EARLY.
